Model labels. Code routes.classify returns a Ticket. pick sends its route field out as the edge to take.

you write def intake(...); ADK wraps it as a FunctionNodeAgent = LlmAgent: one model call
This course is hands-on, and the first picture is the whole idea. The graph is on screen from the start: a Workflow named acme_desk with seven nodes. Press once: the legend. Amber nodes are plain Python functions; you write def intake, and ADK wraps it as a FunctionNode for you, so you never type FunctionNode. Coral nodes are Agent calls; Agent is a type alias of LlmAgent. Press again: classify, the only model call on this path, returns a Ticket object whose route field is "refund"; pick, plain code, sends that value out as the route, so the model produces a value and code picks the edge. Last press: one refund ticket runs START, intake, classify, pick, refund, audit; answer is skipped because pick routed refund. ReAct tool loops are not gone: an LlmAgent with tools still works, Lab 1 uses one, and a Workflow puts it inside a graph. Analogy: the graph is the rail track and the model is a signal operator who reads the ticket; the track decides where the train can go. Likely question: "Is answer a model call too?" Yes, but only on the question path. Next: the same graph in Python, one node at a time.
Preview Lab 3 · Acme support desk · step 1 of 3

The model labels the ticket into a closed set of two routes

labs/adk/c00-acme-desk/acme_desk/agent.py · excerpt 1 of 3
from typing import Literal
from google.adk import Agent, Event, Workflow
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Ticket(BaseModel):
  route: Literal["refund", "question"]
  order_id: str = ""

def intake(node_input: str):
  yield Event(state={"ticket": node_input})

classify = Agent(
    name="classify", output_schema=Ticket,
    instruction="Label refund or question; copy order id: {ticket}")
intakegets the raw text
session.state(empty)ticket = "Refund A-1001, ..."
classifyone model call
Ticketroute="refund"

route is a Literal: the reply can only be refund or question.

A plain def is a node. intake writes the text to session.state.

ADK fills {ticket} from state before the call. No model=: the default is gemini-3.5-flash.

The opening graph as real code, in three excerpts; Lab 3 builds it step by step. The imports are at the top: Agent, Event and Workflow come from google.adk, and Agent is a type alias of LlmAgent. Press once: Ticket is a Pydantic model whose route field is a Literal with two values, and output_schema=Ticket on classify makes the reply validated JSON, so the model cannot invent a third route. Press again: intake is a plain function; ADK wraps it as a FunctionNode. It gets the user's text as node_input and yields an Event with state=, which writes the ticket key into session.state, the dict that every node of this run shares. Press again: classify is the only model call; ADK replaces {ticket} in the instruction with session.state["ticket"] before the call, and a missing key raises a KeyError. There is no model= argument, so the agent uses the 2.13.0 default, gemini-3.5-flash; set model= to pin another id. Analogy: classify fills in a form with two boxes. Likely question: "Where does classify's input come from?" From state through {ticket}; the next slide shows where its output goes.
Preview Lab 3 · Acme support desk · step 2 of 3

Plain code reads the label and picks the route

labs/adk/c00-acme-desk/acme_desk/agent.py · excerpt 2 of 3
def pick(node_input: Ticket):
  yield Event(route=node_input.route,
              output=node_input.model_dump())
Event fieldWhat it does
state=writes keys to session.state
route=picks the outgoing edge
output=becomes the next node's node_input
message=prints text to the user

ADK checks the reply against Ticket and passes pick a Ticket object.

route= picks the edge. The label refund selects the refund branch.

output= becomes refund's node_input: a plain dict.

classifyreturns a Ticket
pickplain code
refundgets a dict
answerAgent
refund question
Excerpt two: what happens between the model and the branches. Press once: pick takes node_input typed as Ticket. ADK validates classify's JSON reply against output_schema=Ticket, and because pick's type hint is the same class, pick gets a Ticket object with a .route attribute; the graph also checks that the two types match when you build it, before any token is spent. Press again: route= on the Event picks the outgoing edge; the label "refund" selects the refund branch and "question" would select answer. Press again: output= is the payload; it becomes the next node's node_input, so refund receives the ticket as a plain dict from model_dump(). The table is the whole Event vocabulary for this course: state= writes shared keys, route= picks an edge, output= feeds the next node, message= prints to the user. Analogy: pick is the clerk who reads the form and drops it in the right tray. Likely question: "Why not let the model call refund as a tool?" Then a prompt decides whether money moves; here code decides, and you can unit-test pick without a model.
Preview Lab 3 · Acme support desk · step 3 of 3

Both branches write one state key, and audit reads it by name

labs/adk/c00-acme-desk/acme_desk/agent.py · excerpt 3 of 3
from google.adk import Agent, Context, Event

def refund(ctx: Context, node_input: dict):
  oid = node_input["order_id"]          # from pick's output=
  ctx.state["outcome"] = f"refund queued for {oid}"
  # returns None; the edge to audit still runs

answer = Agent(
    name="answer", output_key="outcome",
    instruction="Answer in 2 sentences: {ticket}")

def audit(outcome: str):   # not node_input or ctx: read from state
  yield Event(message=f"[audit] {outcome}")
session.state
ticket"Refund A-1001, broken"
outcome"refund queued for A-1001"or answer's reply, on the question path
audit(outcome: str)

refund writes outcome into state. It yields nothing; the edge to audit still runs.

On the question path, answer writes the same key with output_key.

Rule: a parameter that is not node_input or ctx is read from state by its name.

A typo or a missing key stops the run:

error text · google-adk 2.13.0
WorkflowDataError: Missing value for parameter "outcome" of function "audit". It was not found in ... and has no default value.
Excerpt three: how the result reaches audit. The state panel on the right is session.state for one refund run; ticket is already there because intake wrote it. Press once: refund gets the dict that pick sent with output=, and writes outcome into session.state through ctx.state. It yields nothing and returns None; that is allowed, and the edge to audit still runs when refund finishes. Press again: on the question path, answer writes the same key with output_key="outcome", so audit does not care which branch ran. Press again: the rule. audit has one parameter, outcome; it is not node_input and not ctx, so ADK looks it up in session.state by name. That is the default parameter_binding="state". Last press: a typo such as outcom, or a branch that never wrote the key, stops the run with WorkflowDataError; the fix is to match the key or give the parameter a default. Analogy: state is a shared whiteboard; refund writes on it and audit reads it. Likely question: "If both node_input and a state key exist, which one does audit get?" Only the parameter named node_input gets the edge payload; every other name comes from state.
Preview Lab 3 · Acme support desk · wire and run

Three kinds of edge entry wire the whole graph

labs/adk/c00-acme-desk/acme_desk/agent.py · last lines
from google.adk import Workflow

root_agent = Workflow(name="acme_desk", edges=[
    ("START", intake, classify, pick),
    (pick, {"refund": refund, "question": answer}),
    (refund, audit), (answer, audit)])

A tuple of N nodes is a chain. "START" is a reserved name, valid only in a chain.

A dict maps each route label to a node. A label with no key runs nothing; Lab 3 adds a default.

Two pairs join both branches at audit.

Run it from the parent folder. Only events with message= print.

terminal · output illustrative
$ adk run acme_desk "Refund A-1001, broken"
[acme_desk]: [audit] refund queued for A-1001
START
intake
classify
pick
refund
answer
audit
refund question
The last lines of the file wire everything together, and the graph below lights up the part of the graph that each entry creates. Press once: a tuple of N nodes is a chain; START, intake, classify and pick run in that order. "START" is a reserved name, and the string form works only inside a chain tuple; elsewhere import START from google.adk.workflow. Press again: a pair of a node and a dict is a route map; each key is a route label and each value is the node that runs. A label with no key runs nothing and raises no error; the log only says "The branch will end." That is why Ticket uses a Literal, and why Lab 3 adds DEFAULT_ROUTE and a test for it. Press again: two plain pairs, refund to audit and answer to audit, join the branches. Last press: run it from the parent folder of acme_desk; the quoted text is the first user message. Only events with message= print, and function nodes print under the workflow name, so you see one line. The output is illustrative. Likely question: "Does order inside the list matter?" No; the entries describe edges, not steps.

Pin the exact version: behaviour changed between 2.x minor releases.

pip must show 2.13.0. The API key goes in .env: next slide.

Do this once before Lab 1; the same steps are in labs/adk/c00-acme-desk/README.md. Press once: check that Python is 3.11 or newer, because google-adk 2.12.0 raised the minimum and many macOS and Ubuntu LTS machines still default to an older Python; on Windows the command is python, not python3. Then make a virtual environment. Press again: activate it with the line for your OS; in cmd.exe the command is .venv\Scripts\activate.bat. Press again: pin google-adk to exactly 2.13.0. Thirteen minor releases shipped between 2.0.0 on 19 May and 2.13.0 on 23 October, and behaviour changed between them; for example, 2.10.0 stopped filling ${var} placeholders in instructions. The labs were checked against 2.13.0 only. Last press: pip show must say 2.13.0, and adk --help proves the CLI is on your PATH. The output is trimmed and illustrative; pip show prints more lines such as Summary and Location. We do not export the API key here: it goes in a .env file, which works the same on every OS. Analogy: pinning is like a recipe that names the exact flour, so every student gets the same cake. Likely question: "Can I use uv instead of pip?" Yes; pin the same version.
Gotcha setup · any OS · google-adk 2.13.0

Put the key in acme_desk/.env under the new switch name

acme_desk/ run adk from its parent __init__.py from . import agent agent.py the graph: root_agent .env adk run and adk web load it
acme_desk/.env
GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE=FALSE
GOOGLE_API_KEY=<key from aistudio.google.com>

FALSE: use the API key, not a Cloud project. Add .env to .gitignore.

SymptomA DeprecationWarning on start. CauseOld tutorials set GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI. 2.x renamed it. FixDelete that line. Keep GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE.
Repo adk-python v2.13.0 · utils/env_utils.py
One file holds the key on every OS, so we do not export anything in the shell. The folder tree is the agent package: __init__.py contains exactly one line, from . import agent, agent.py defines root_agent, and you run adk from the parent folder. Press once: the .env file sits inside the agent folder; adk run and adk web load it automatically, so you do not call load_dotenv yourself, and each agent folder has its own .env. FALSE means "use the AI Studio key, not a Cloud project". No quotes are needed around the key. Add .env to .gitignore: committing a key is the real Monday risk. The lab folder ships acme_desk/.env.example; copy it to .env. Press again: you will see GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI in older tutorials and codelabs. In google-adk 2.x that name still works but raises a DeprecationWarning (utils/env_utils.py), and GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE wins if both are set. Last press: the fix points at the line to keep. Analogy: a renamed light switch still works, but the electrician leaves a note on it. Likely question: "Should I commit .env?" No; commit .env.example and keep the key out of git.

Your first agent

Build the Acme refund desk: two tools, a runner, a refund cap and a human approval gate.

2 typed tools + a runner callbacks: refund cap + PII human approval over $200 google-adk 2.13.0
This chapter builds one agent end to end: the Acme refund desk that answers "Can I return order A-1002?". We start with an LlmAgent on gemini-3.5-flash and two typed Python functions, lookup_order and check_refund_eligibility, then drive it from adk run, adk web and a Python runner with full trajectory logs. Next we move policy out of the prompt: callbacks enforce the refund cap and redact PII, and FunctionTool with require_confirmation stops refunds over $200 until a human says yes. Analogy: the instruction is the job description, the tools are the forms the clerk can fill, and the callbacks are the till that refuses a refund over the limit no matter what the clerk was told. Likely question: "Why not just write the cap in the prompt?" Because a prompt can be talked around, and a callback is code that runs every time. Everything in this chapter is tested on google-adk 2.13.0. All lab code is in labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools and labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails. Lab 1 starts on the next slide with the setup.

Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 2 of 8

The signature and the docstring become the schema the model reads

labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field

def lookup_order(
    order_id: Annotated[str, Field(description="Order ID, e.g. A-1001")],
) -> dict:
    """Look up an order.

    Always call this before answering a refund question."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id.strip().upper())
    if order is None:
        return {"status": "error",
                "error_message": f"No order with ID {order_id}."}
    return {"status": "success", "order": order}
tool schema · what the model reads
lookup_order
order_id.description"Order ID, e.g. A-1001"
description"Look up an order. Always call this before answering…"
returnsa dict · errors are data too

Field(description=...) describes one parameter.

The whole docstring becomes the tool description. ADK does not parse an Args: section.

Return a dict. Any other value arrives as {'result': value}.

Codelab Building AI Agents with ADK: Empowering with Tools
The model never sees your Python. It sees a schema built from the signature and the docstring. Step 1: Annotated with Field(description=...) gives order_id its own description. Step 2: the whole cleaned docstring becomes the tool description, verbatim; ADK does not parse a Google-style Args: section, so per-parameter text goes in Field. The codelab says it plainly: "The LLM uses the docstring to decide when and how to call the tool." Step 3: return a dict, also for errors, so the model can read the error and recover; any non-dict value is wrapped as {'result': value}. Analogy: the docstring is the label on a drawer; the model never opens the drawer, it only reads the label. Likely question: "Where do I say when not to call the tool?" In the docstring: when to call it, what it returns, what it will not do. Next: the second tool and the agent.
Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 3 of 8

A Literal type becomes an enum, and plain functions become tools

labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
from typing import Literal
from google.adk import Agent

Reason = Literal["changed_mind", "damaged", "wrong_item"]

def check_refund_eligibility(
    order_id: str, reason: Reason = "changed_mind"
) -> dict:
    """Apply the refund policy: 30-day window. ..."""
    # ... window check: see the lab file

root_agent = Agent(
    name="refund_agent", model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    instruction=INSTRUCTION,  # quote the rule; never promise a refund
    tools=[lookup_order, check_refund_eligibility],
)
check_refund_eligibility · schema
reason.enum
changed_minddamagedwrong_item
reason: optional (has a default)
refund_agentLlmAgent
tools=[lookup_ordercheck_refund_…]

The model can only pick one of the three reasons. It cannot invent "broken".

A default makes reason optional. A parameter without one is mandatory.

Pass plain functions in tools=[...]. The name must be a Python identifier.

Step 1: Literal becomes an enum in the schema, so the model can only choose changed_mind, damaged or wrong_item; it cannot invent "broken". Step 2: reason has a default, so it is optional; order_id has none, so it is mandatory, and if the model omits it ADK returns an error dict instead of raising. Step 3: the agent is one constructor call; plain functions go straight into tools and ADK wraps each one in a FunctionTool. The name refund_agent must be a Python identifier and must not be "user". The full check_refund_eligibility body, the window logic and the three demo orders A-1001 to A-1003 are in labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools. Analogy: the enum is a drop-down list on a form; the clerk cannot type a new value. Likely question: "Does the instruction still matter?" Yes, it sets the order of calls and the rule quoting; the tools set what is possible. Next: run it.
Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 4 of 8

adk run shows the tool calls behind each refund answer

terminal · folder that contains refund_agent/
$ adk run refund_agent \
    "Can I return order A-1002? I just changed my mind."
$ adk run refund_agent           # interactive
$ adk run refund_agent --in_memory --jsonl \

Audit the trajectory, not only the answer. A right answer can hide a wrong process.

trajectory · one turn · illustrative
user "Can I return order A-1002? I just changed my mind."
function_call lookup_order(order_id="A-1002") → category "electronics", 41 days
function_call check_refund_eligibility(order_id="A-1002", reason="changed_mind") → eligible: false, window_days: 30 41 > 30
final answer "…our policy allows change-of-mind returns within 30 days, so it is not eligible."
Run every command from the folder that contains refund_agent, not from inside it, because ADK imports the folder as a Python package. The one-shot form takes the query as a positional argument; without it adk run is interactive; --in_memory --jsonl gives a clean, scriptable run. Walk the trajectory on the right: the user message, lookup_order, then check_refund_eligibility, where 41 days is more than the 30-day window, and only then the final answer, which quotes the rule from the tool result. Analogy: the trajectory is the receipt for the answer; the answer is the total, the tool calls are the line items you audit. Likely question: "Why not just test the final text?" Because a correct answer can hide a wrong process; the CXBench paper on the runner slides puts a number on that. Next: the same events in adk web, including an error.
Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 5 of 8

Tool errors come back to the model as data, so it can retry

127.0.0.1:8000 · refund_agent · illustrativeEvents
→function_callcheck_refund_eligibility(reason="changed_mind")
←function_response"Invoking `check_refund_eligibility()` failed as the following mandatory input parameters are not present: ..."
→function_call retrycheck_refund_eligibility(order_id="A-1002", reason="changed_mind")
←function_response{"eligible": false, "window_days": 30}
terminal
$ adk web --port 8000
# open http://127.0.0.1:8000
# pick refund_agent, then Events

A missing mandatory argument does not raise. ADK sends the error text to the model.

SymptomEdits do not reload on Windows. Cause--reload is not supported on Windows ... Forcing --no-reload. FixExpected. Restart adk web after each edit.
adk web serves the dev UI on 127.0.0.1:8000 by default; pick refund_agent and open the Events tab to see every call and response of a turn. Step 1: suppose the model forgets order_id. Step 2: ADK does not raise; it returns the text "Invoking `check_refund_eligibility()` failed as the following mandatory input parameters are not present: ..." to the model as the tool result. Step 3: the model reads it and retries with the missing argument. These rows are illustrative: the error text is exact, the sequence is an example. Step 4: on Windows adk web prints "WARNING: The --reload flag is not supported on Windows because it forces Uvicorn to use SelectorEventLoop, which does not support subprocesses (needed for executing tools). Forcing --no-reload." So restart the server after each edit. Analogy: a form with a missing field comes back to the clerk with a sticky note, not to the shredder. Likely question: "Should my own tools raise?" No: return {"status": "error", "error_message": ...} so the model can explain or retry. Next: drive the agent from Python.
Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 6 of 8

InMemoryRunner and run_debug drive the agent from Python

python run_refund.pynext to refund_agent/
labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/run_refund.py · excerpt
import asyncio
from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner
from refund_agent.agent import root_agent

APP = "refund_agent"   # match the folder name

async def main() -> None:
    runner = InMemoryRunner(agent=root_agent, app_name=APP)
    await runner.run_debug(
        "Is order A-1001 refundable? Changed my mind.",
        verbose=True)
    # ... run_async loop and isolation: next slides
    await runner.close()

One line gives in-memory session, artifact and memory services.

run_debug() creates a session and prints each event. It is "for debugging and experimentation only".

Close the runner. It is also an async context manager.

InMemoryRunner bundles an in-memory session service, artifact service and memory service in one line. Its app_name must equal the folder name, or ADK warns "App name mismatch detected" and later sessions are not found. Step 2: run_debug gets or creates the session debug_session_id for user debug_user_id, wraps your string as a user message, prints every event and returns the list of events; its own docstring says it is for debugging and experimentation only. Step 3: await runner.close() closes plugins; you can also use async with. Analogy: run_debug is the test bench with the cover off; run_async, on the next slide, is the engine in the car. Likely question: "Why does my output show [Calling tool: ...] lines?" That is verbose=True, which prints tool calls and results. The output is illustrative: the shape follows the printing code, the wording will differ. Next: the production loop.
Lab 1 Acme refund desk · step 7 of 8

Log every event from run_async: the trajectory is where agents fail

labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/run_refund.py · excerpt
    session = await runner.session_service.create_session(
        app_name=APP, user_id="cust-dana")
    msg = types.UserContent(parts=[types.Part(
        text="Is A-1003 refundable? It arrived damaged.")])
    async for event in runner.run_async(
            user_id="cust-dana", session_id=session.id, new_message=msg):
        for call in event.get_function_calls():
            print(f"  TOOL CALL  {call.name}({call.args})")
        for resp in event.get_function_responses():
            print(f"  TOOL RESULT {resp.name} -> {resp.response}")
        final = event.is_final_response()
        if final and event.content and event.content.parts:
            text = "".join(p.text or "" for p in event.content.parts)
            print(f"[{event.author}] {text}")

Create the session first, under the same app_name.

run_async() is the production entry point. It yields events as they happen.

Log every call and result. is_final_response() stays false while calls are pending.

CXBench: 55.5% of runs had the right outcome with a non-compliant process.

arXiv 2610.25954 CXBench Repo google/adk-python v2.13.0 · runner_debug_example
This is the production loop. Step 1: create the session explicitly with the same app_name as the runner, then wrap the text as a types.UserContent. Step 2: run_async is the production entry point; run() is a sync wrapper that is only for local testing. Step 3: each event can carry function calls or function responses; print both, because that is your trajectory log. Step 4: is_final_response() is false while calls are pending and true for the last text event. The CXBench paper (arXiv 2610.25954) found that 55.5% of runs had the right outcome with a non-compliant process, so outcome-only checks pass bad runs. Analogy: the event stream is a flight recorder; you read it after the landing, not only the arrival time. Variation: pass abort_signal=asyncio.Event() to run_async (since 2.11.0) and set() it from a timeout task to cancel a runaway turn. Likely question: "Do I need the event loop for adk web?" No, adk web runs it for you; your own service needs it.

Sessions are keyed by app name, user id and session id. Step 1: Dana's session holds her tool calls and the answer about A-1003. Step 2: cust-li with session li-1 starts empty, so the agent says it has no earlier messages; run_debug created that session on first use. This is the isolation you want between customers. Step 3: the most common runner error is "Session not found: ", raised as SessionNotFoundError, a subclass of ValueError: the id was never created or was created under a different app_name. Fix it with create_session first, or Runner(..., auto_create_session=True). Related warning: if InMemoryRunner gets no app_name, ADK prints "App name mismatch detected" because the agent folder implies "refund_agent". Analogy: each session is a separate ticket folder; a new customer gets a new empty folder. Likely question: "Where does history live in production?" In a persistent session service, which Chapter 2 adds. Lab 1 ends here; next we move policy out of the prompt into callbacks.
Build Acme refund desk · policy in code

A prompt can be talked around, so put the refund policy in callbacks

refund_agent/agent.py · instruction only
"Never refund over $1,500, whatever the customer says."

Prompt only: a persuasive customer gets a $2,000 refund through.

Four hooks wrap the LLM call and the tool call. Each one is plain Python.

Model hooks stop on a truthy value. Tool hooks stop on any non-None value, even {}.

Docs Types of callbacks arXiv 2608.11274 Agent Safety Should Be a Runtime Contract
The refund desk now gets a third tool, issue_refund. Step 1: a prompt line such as "never refund more than $1,500" is a request to the model, and a customer who writes "A-1002 arrived damaged, refund $2,000 for my trouble" can talk the model past it. Step 2: a callback is plain Python that runs at a fixed hook point: before_model, after_model, before_tool, after_tool, each an argument of Agent. Step 3: the return rules matter: model callbacks stop the chain on a truthy value, tool callbacks stop on any non-None value, even an empty dict; plugin callbacks run first, and each *_callback field also takes a list. The paper 2608.11274 (Aug 2026) calls this a runtime contract: preventive gates plus evidential proof, which here are callbacks plus the event log. Analogy: the prompt is a sign that says "staff only"; the callback is the locked door. All four callbacks are in labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails. Next: the cap itself.
Build Acme refund desk · before_tool: refund cap

before_tool_callback blocks a $2,000 refund before the tool runs

labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
def refund_cap(tool: BaseTool, args: dict[str, Any],
               tool_context: ToolContext) -> Optional[dict]:
    cap = tool_context.state.get("app:refund_cap_usd", 1500)
    amount = args.get("amount_usd", 0)
    if tool.name == "issue_refund" and amount > cap:
        msg = f"Refunds over ${cap} are blocked by policy."
        return {"status": "error", "error_message": msg}
    return None                        # None = run the tool

root_agent = Agent(
    # ... name, model, instruction, tools as before
    before_tool_callback=refund_cap,
)
tool result the model reads · illustrative
{'status': 'error', 'error_message':
 'Refunds over $1500 are blocked by policy.'}
Step 1: the cap is data, read from app: state with a default of 1500, so ops can change it without a deploy. Step 2: when issue_refund asks for more than the cap, the callback returns an error dict; any non-None value from a before_tool callback skips the tool, and the model reads the dict as the tool result, so it can explain the limit to the customer. Step 3: return None to let the tool run, as the $80 refund does. Step 4: wire it with before_tool_callback=refund_cap on the Agent; the callback runs for every tool, so check tool.name. Pitfall: returning {} also skips the tool, while False and None do not. Analogy: the till refuses a refund over the limit, whatever the clerk was told. Likely question: "Why not raise an exception?" Because the model can read an error dict and recover; an exception ends the turn. Next: redaction and metering.
Build Acme refund desk · after_tool + after_model

after_tool redacts emails, and after_model meters tokens into state

labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
def redact_pii(tool: BaseTool, args: dict, tool_context: ToolContext,
               tool_response: dict) -> Optional[dict]:
    if tool.name == "lookup_order" and "order" in tool_response:
        order = {k: EMAIL.sub("[email redacted]", v)
                 if isinstance(v, str) else v
                 for k, v in tool_response["order"].items()}
        return {**tool_response, "order": order}
    return None                     # None = keep the tool result

def meter_tokens(callback_context: Context,
                 llm_response: LlmResponse) -> Optional[LlmResponse]:
    if llm_response.usage_metadata:
        used = callback_context.state.get("tokens_used", 0)
        callback_context.state["tokens_used"] = used + (
            llm_response.usage_metadata.total_token_count or 0)
    return None                     # None = keep the response

li@example.com[email redacted]

The fourth hook, block_card_numbers, stops card numbers before the model. It is in the lab file.

Step 1: after_tool_callback sees the tool's response; a non-None return value replaces it, so the model never sees the customer's email, only "[email redacted]". Return None for every other tool to keep the original result. Step 2: after_model_callback runs after each model call; it adds usage_metadata.total_token_count to tokens_used in session state. A state write inside a callback goes into the event's state_delta, so it is persisted like any other state change. The number is illustrative. Step 3: the fourth hook, before_model_callback=block_card_numbers, checks the last user turn for a card number and returns a canned LlmResponse, so the model is never called; the code is in labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails. Pitfall: before_model only sees the request; injected text can also arrive inside a tool result, which is one more reason for after_tool checks. Analogy: redaction is the black marker on the copy, the meter is the electricity meter on the wall. Likely question: "Why not redact in the tool?" You can, but a callback applies one rule to every tool and every agent you attach it to.
Build Acme refund desk · human approval over $200

Gate refunds over $200 with require_confirmation, not a prompt line

labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool, ToolContext

APPROVAL_THRESHOLD_USD = 200.0

def needs_approval(order_id: str, amount_usd: float,
                   tool_context: ToolContext) -> bool:
    """Same parameters as issue_refund. ..."""
    return amount_usd > APPROVAL_THRESHOLD_USD

root_agent = Agent(
    # ... name, model, instruction, callbacks as before
    tools=[lookup_order, check_refund_eligibility,
           FunctionTool(issue_refund,
                        require_confirmation=needs_approval)],
)

Prompt only: "ask a supervisor first" is a request. The model ran all three refunds.

ADK calls the predicate with the tool's own arguments. It must return a real bool.

Wrap the tool. Over $200 the call stops until a human answers.

Repo adk-python v2.13.0 · tools/function_tool.py
The cap from the last build is a hard ceiling at $1,500. Between $200 and $1,500 Acme wants a person to decide. Step 1: an instruction such as "ask a supervisor before any refund over $200" is only a request to the model; nothing stops the call, so all three refunds ran. Step 2: require_confirmation takes a bool or a predicate; ADK calls needs_approval with the tool's own arguments, unfiltered, so the predicate must take the same parameter names, including tool_context, or Python raises a TypeError about an unexpected keyword argument. Step 3: wrap issue_refund in FunctionTool; $80 is issued at once, $250 and $1,299 wait. The issue_refund body writes refunds_issued to state, so approved refunds are auditable; it is in labs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails. Analogy: the predicate is the till that calls the manager for any refund over the limit. Likely question: "Can the model skip the gate?" No: the gate is in FunctionTool, not in the prompt. Next: what the human and the model see.
Build Acme refund desk · approve or reject

adk run asks a human, and a no reaches the model as an error

adk run refund_agentlabs/adk/lab1-refund-guardrails
adk run refund_agent · output · illustrative
[user]: A-1002 arrived damaged. Refund the $1,299.
[HITL confirm] Please approve or reject the tool call
  issue_refund() by responding with a FunctionResponse
  with an expected ToolConfirmation payload.
  Type "yes" to confirm, anything else to reject.

what the model reads
first call · tool result"This tool call requires confirmation, please approve or reject."
after "no" · tool result"This tool call is rejected."
SymptomA large refund runs with no prompt. CauseThe predicate fell through and returned None, which skips the gate. Issue #7010, open. FixAlways return a real bool.
Issue google/adk-python #7010
Step 1: over $200 the first call does not run the tool; ADK calls request_confirmation and returns the error dict "This tool call requires confirmation, please approve or reject." adk run detects the pending long-running call and prints the [HITL confirm] prompt; y, yes, true and confirm count as yes. Step 2: anything else is a rejection, and the model reads "This tool call is rejected."; the instruction tells it to say a supervisor declined, so it does not pretend the refund went through. adk web shows a dialog instead. In your own client, watch event.long_running_tool_ids and send back a FunctionResponse with the same id and {"confirmed": true} or {"confirmed": false}. Step 3: the open issue #7010: a predicate that falls off a branch returns None, None is falsy, and the gate is skipped; always return a real bool. Analogy: the manager's key must be turned one way or the other; "no answer" must never mean yes. Likely question: "Can the approver change the amount?" That needs the request-input HITL path, which Chapter 5 covers. Next: the three errors that stop most first runs.
Gotcha First run · the loader

The loader needs a package name and a variable called root_agent

SymptomInvalid agent name: 'refund-agent'. Agent names must be valid Python identifiers (letters, digits, and underscores only). CauseADK imports the folder as a Python package. A hyphen breaks the import. FixUse refund_agent for the folder and for name=. Never name an agent user.
SymptomNo root_agent found for 'refund_agent'. Searched in 'refund_agent.agent.root_agent', 'refund_agent.root_agent' and 'refund_agent/root_agent.yaml'. CauseThe variable is called agent, or __init__.py lost from . import agent. FixName it root_agent (or app, Chapter 2). Keep the scaffolded __init__.py.
layout that adk run and adk web load
refund_agent/     # folder = package
  __init__.py     # from . import agent
  agent.py        # defines root_agent
  .env            # GOOGLE_API_KEY=...
Two of the three errors that stop most first runs come from the loader, before any model call. Step 1: adk run and adk web import the agent folder as a Python package, then look for a variable called root_agent. Step 2: a hyphen in the folder gives "Invalid agent name: 'refund-agent'. Agent names must be valid Python identifiers"; a hyphen in name= gives the sibling error "Found invalid agent name: `refund-agent`. Agent name must be a valid identifier...". The name user is also reserved. Step 3: "No root_agent found for 'refund_agent'" lists the three places the loader searched: agent.root_agent, the package itself and root_agent.yaml. The fix is to name the variable root_agent, or app for an App (Chapter 2), and keep from . import agent in __init__.py. Analogy: the loader is a courier with one address format; a hyphen or a different door name and the parcel comes back. Likely question: "Can I keep a hyphenated repo name?" Yes, the repo can have any name; only the agent folder must be an identifier. Next: the third error, a loop that hits the call cap.
Gotcha First run · the runner

A tool-call loop runs to the 500-call cap, so set a lower cap

SymptomMax number of llm calls limit of `500` exceeded CauseThe model calls a tool again and again in one run. Vague tool errors make it worse. FixReturn clear error dicts. Lower the cap per run.
labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/run_capped.py · excerpt
from google.adk.agents.run_config import RunConfig
# ... inside main(): runner, session, msg as before
    cfg = RunConfig(max_llm_calls=20)  # or ADK_MAX_LLM_CALLS=20
    async for ev in runner.run_async(
            user_id="cust-dana", session_id=session.id,
            new_message=msg, run_config=cfg):
default cap · 5000LLM calls in one run
RunConfig · max_llm_calls=200LLM calls in one run
Repo google/adk-python v2.13.0 · agents/run_config.py
The third first-run error comes from the runner. Step 1: the symptom is LlmCallsLimitExceededError with the text "Max number of llm calls limit of `500` exceeded": the model called a tool again and again in one run, often because the tool returned a vague error. Step 2: the default cap is 500 LLM calls per run, so a loop burns 500 calls before it stops. Step 3: set RunConfig(max_llm_calls=20) on run_async, or the ADK_MAX_LLM_CALLS environment variable, so a loop fails fast and cheap at 20; then read the logged tool calls to find the loop. The excerpt is in labs/adk/lab1-refund-tools/run_capped.py. Analogy: the call cap is a circuit breaker; it protects the bill, it does not fix the wiring. Likely question: "Is 20 enough?" The refund desk needs three or four calls per turn; size the cap to a few times your longest normal trajectory. Next: the temperature trap.

    temperature=0,          # not an Agent field
    # ...
)

from google.genai import types

root_agent = Agent(
    name="refund_agent", model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=1.0),   # the Gemini 3 default

"Changing the temperature (setting it below 1.0) may lead to unexpected behavior, such as looping or degraded performance."

Docs Gemini 3 developer guide
Step 1: many first agents copy temperature=0 from older tutorials and pass it straight to Agent. Step 2: ADK rejects it with a pydantic ValidationError: "temperature is a GenerateContentConfig field. Pass generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=...) instead." Step 3: sampling settings belong in generate_content_config. Step 4: on Gemini 3 do not lower the temperature at all: the Gemini 3 developer guide says that setting it below 1.0 "may lead to unexpected behavior, such as looping or degraded performance". That links straight back to the last gotcha: a lower temperature can cause the loop that hits the call cap. Analogy: the agent is the driver, the GenerateContentConfig is the engine map; you tune the engine in its own menu. Likely question: "How do I make answers deterministic, then?" Put the decision in tools and callbacks, which are deterministic code, and test the trajectory, not the wording. Next: two October papers on tool descriptions.
arXiv Oct 2026 · tool descriptions

Inflated tool descriptions cut task success from 89% to ~30%

arXiv 2610.28454 2026-10-20

Toolflation: Seller Agents Distort Tool Markets Through Spontaneous Generative Engine Optimization

Seller agents over-claim in tool descriptions. Buyer agents then pick by list position. Task success fell from 89% to ~30% under one model.
Write specific docstrings: when to call, what returns, what it will not do. Review third-party tool text before you load it.
arXiv 2610.28454 Toolflation
The tool description is part of your accuracy and part of your attack surface. Step 1: in Toolflation (arXiv 2610.28454, 20 Oct 2026), seller agents write tool descriptions, and they spontaneously over-claim, so every tool says it is the best. Step 2: buyer agents stop reading and pick by list position; under one model, task success fell from 89% to about 30%. The animation is a schematic of that finding, not the paper's own figure. Step 3: the Monday change for Acme is cheap: keep each docstring specific about when to call the tool, what it returns and what it will not do, with no ranking claims, and review the descriptions of any third-party or MCP tools before you load them. Analogy: when every product on the shelf says "number one", shoppers grab the one at eye level. Likely question: "Does ADK rank tools?" No: the model reads the descriptions in the request; ADK passes them through verbatim. Next: a paper on what to do when tool interfaces drift.
arXiv Oct 2026 · interface drift

Validate, retry, repair: tool-call accuracy rose from 0.580 to 0.805

arXiv 2610.23342 2026-10-16

Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift

A training-free layer, SchemaShield-Lite, raised BFCL-200 accuracy from 0.580 to 0.805 on Qwen3.5-9B. Distractor tools did most of the damage.
Keep the Acme tool list short. Validate arguments in before_tool_callback, as refund_cap does.
arXiv 2610.23342 Interface Drift
Step 1: interface drift means the tool schema the model learned is not the schema it gets: renamed fields, new enums, extra tools. Step 2: the paper (arXiv 2610.23342, 16 Oct 2026) wraps each call in a training-free validate, retry and repair layer, SchemaShield-Lite: validate the arguments against the schema, ask the model to retry, repair what is still wrong, then run the tool. On BFCL-200 with Qwen3.5-9B, accuracy rose from 0.580 to 0.805, and distractor tools did most of the damage. The token in the animation is an illustrative argument: "broken" is not in the Literal enum, so validation fails and the repair gives "damaged". Step 3: for Acme, keep the three tools, and put argument checks in before_tool_callback, as refund_cap does. Analogy: a form checker at the counter sends the form back before the clerk files it. Likely question: "Does ADK do this validation for me?" The Literal enum and the mandatory-argument check catch some errors; semantic checks are your callback's job. Next: two production teams that got better results with fewer tools.
In production Vercel · d0 text-to-SQL agent

Vercel cut its agent from 17 tools to 2 and got 3.5x faster

77.4 s
5 queries · was 274.8 s
61k
tokens · was ~102k
Only 5 queries. It worked because the semantic layer was well documented.
Blog Vercel: We removed 80% of our agent's tools
Vercel's d0 agent answers data questions with SQL (post of 2025-12-22). Step 1: version 1 had 17 specialised tools; version 2 gives the model two general tools, ExecuteCommand and ExecuteSQL, and lets it grep a well-documented semantic layer of YAML, Markdown and JSON. Step 2: on their 5 test queries it went from 274.8 to 77.4 seconds, from 4 of 5 to 5 of 5 correct, from about 102k to 61k tokens, and from about 12 to 7 steps; the worst old run took 724 seconds, 100 steps and 145,463 tokens and still failed. Step 3: be honest about the caveat: five queries is an anecdote, and the trick only works when the data is documented well enough to search. Analogy: a junior with two sharp tools and a good manual beats one with a drawer of 17 gadgets. Likely question: "So should I merge the three refund desk tools?" No: keep them; add or merge tools only when an eval shows a measured gain. Next: Shopify's tool-count bands.
In production Shopify · Sidekick

Shopify found that tool boundaries blur past 20 tools

Fix: return just-in-time instructions with the tool results. The cached system prompt stays stable.

Acme: keep the three tools. Add a tool only when an eval shows it helps.

Blog Shopify: Building production-ready agentic systems
Shopify's Sidekick team (engineering post of 2025-08-26) published rough tool-count bands. Step 1: under 20 tools the boundaries between tools are clear; from 20 to 50 they blur; past 50 the model finds many ways to do the same task. Step 2: the Acme refund desk sits at 3 tools; Vercel's d0 v1 sat at 17, near the edge of the clear band, and still got faster with 2. Step 3: Shopify's fix was not a bigger system prompt: they return just-in-time instructions with the tool results, so guidance arrives where it is needed and the cached system prompt stays stable. Step 4: the lesson for Acme: keep the three tools and add one only when an eval shows a measured gain. Analogy: a toolbox with labelled drawers works until two drawers say "fasteners". Likely question: "What if I really need 60 tools?" Then split them behind skills or a toolset filter so the model sees only the ones a task needs, which Chapters 6 and 7 cover. Chapter 2 moves to the Acme claims desk: structured output, state and sessions.
02

Structured output, state and the App

By the end, adk api_server serves the claims App on :8000, and sessions live in a SQLite file.

This chapter builds one service in five steps, in this order: typed intake with output_schema, an App with an audit plugin, the same App over REST and SSE with adk api_server, state scopes that remember the customer, and sessions in a SQLite file that survive a restart. Each later step adds one file to the same lab folder, so point at the road map when you start each step. It is Lab 2 because Lab 1 was the refund desk in chapter 1. Analogy: the App is a shipping container; the agent is the cargo, and plugins, config and state go in the same box. A likely question is "Why not call the model with a JSON schema directly?" Because the App gives you state, plugins and a server, and the schema result lands in state where the next agent can read it. Everything is tested against google-adk 2.13.0 with Python 3.11 or newer. The complete files live in labs/adk/lab2-claims-api; the slides show only the lines that carry each idea, and the next slide sets the folder up.

This is the run-it-Monday slide for Lab 2. Create one virtual environment, install google-adk 2.13.0 (Python 3.11 or newer), and export two variables: GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE=0 selects an AI Studio key, 1 selects Agent Platform, the former Vertex AI. Walk the folder tree in three clicks. First, claims/ holds plain Python scripts; they run outside adk web, so they do not read a .env file and you must export the variables. Second, agents/claims_api/ is the App folder; its __init__.py says "from . import agent", and adk run, adk web and adk api_server load it and do read its .env. Third, rest_calls.sh holds the curl calls for step 3; PowerShell breaks the single-quoted JSON, so use Git Bash or WSL on Windows. Analogy: this folder is the workbench; every later slide picks up one tool from it. A likely question: "Can I use Python 3.10?" No: google-adk 2.13.0 requires 3.11, even though the quickstart page still says 3.10.
Lab 2 Acme claims API · step 1 of 3

A Pydantic schema tells the model which claim fields to fill

python claims/claim_intake.py claims/email_77.txt
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claim_intake.py · excerpt
class ClaimIntake(BaseModel):
    reasoning: str = Field(
        description="One sentence: the facts behind the labels.")
    claim_type: Literal["auto_collision", "auto_glass", "home_water",
                        "home_theft", "other"]
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] = Field(
        description="low < $2k, medium $2k-$10k, high = injury or > $10k")
    policy_number: Optional[str] = Field(
        None, description="POL-######, or null")
    incident_date: Optional[str] = Field(
        None, description="YYYY-MM-DD, or null if unknown")
    estimated_loss_usd: Optional[float] = None
    injuries_reported: bool

The schema is the claim form. The model fills it from the email.

reasoning comes first: the model writes why before it picks a label.

Literal closes each label set. The description gives the money bands.

The email has no year, so incident_date stays null. Never guess.

No, the model reads it as a second prompt, so keep it consistent with the instruction.

intake_agent = Agent(
    name="claim_intake",
    model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    instruction=("Extract a ClaimIntake from the email. "
                 "Never guess a value."),
    output_schema=ClaimIntake,     # not generate_content_config
    output_key="claim",
)
# ...
async def main(email: str) -> None:
    runner = InMemoryRunner(agent=intake_agent, app_name="claims_api")
    await runner.run_debug(email, quiet=True)
    s = await runner.session_service.get_session(
        app_name="claims_api",
        user_id="debug_user_id", session_id="debug_session_id")
    claim = s.state["claim"]            # a dict, None fields dropped

Same file, second half: the agent and the run. Click 1: output_schema validates the model reply against ClaimIntake, and output_key names the state key, here "claim". Click 2: run_debug creates its own session with user_id "debug_user_id" and session_id "debug_session_id", which is why get_session uses those ids. Click 3: state receives a plain dict from model_dump(exclude_none=True), so the null incident_date is not in state at all; read optional keys with .get(), and call ClaimIntake.model_validate(claim) when you want the typed object back. The gotcha slide later shows the KeyError this causes. Analogy: the clerk files a copy of the form and leaves out the empty boxes. A likely question: "Why not keep the pydantic object in state?" State must be JSON-serialisable so every session service can store it, so ADK stores a dict.
Lab 2 Acme claims API · step 2 of 3

A plugin hook sees every tool call before the tool runs

adk run agents/claims_api
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/agents/claims_api/agent.py · excerpt
def lookup_policy(policy_number: str) -> dict:
    """Return coverage for a policy number like POL-448120."""
    return {"status": "success", "policy_number": policy_number,
            "collision_deductible_usd": 500,
            "coverage": ["collision", "glass", "liability"]}

class AuditPlugin(BasePlugin):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(name="audit")
    async def before_tool_callback(
            self, *, tool: BaseTool, tool_args: dict[str, Any],
            tool_context: ToolContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        log = tool_context.state.get("audit_log", [])
        entry = f"{tool.name}({tool_args})"
        tool_context.state["audit_log"] = log + [entry]
        return None                     # None: the tool runs

A plugin is a class with hooks. The App registers it once for every agent.

lookup_policy returns a dict. The model reads the deductible: 500.

Plugin hooks are keyword-only. This hook appends one audit_log entry.

Return None: the tool runs. Return a dict: it replaces the tool result.

claims_assistantgemini-3.5-flash
AuditPluginbefore_tool_callback
session.stateaudit_log: []audit_log: 1 entry
lookup_policydeductible 500
Step 1 extracted the claim. Now a second agent, claims_assistant, answers coverage questions, and the App in agents/claims_api/agent.py adds an audit plugin. The two agents are joined in a later chapter, so for now the user types the policy number. Click 1: the tool returns a plain dict; the model reads collision_deductible_usd 500. Click 2: the plugin hook is keyword-only, and it uses tool_args, not args as an agent callback does; it appends one audit entry to state before every tool call, in every agent of the App. Click 3: returning None lets the tool run; returning a dict would skip the tool and use that dict as the result. Analogy: the plugin is the security desk in the lobby: every visitor signs the book, whichever floor they go to. A likely question: "Plugin or agent callback?" Use a plugin for rules that must cover every agent; plugins run before agent callbacks, and the first non-None result wins.
Lab 2 Acme claims API · step 2 of 3

An App bundles the agent and its plugins into one deployable unit

labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/agents/claims_api/agent.py · excerpt
from google.adk import Agent
from google.adk.apps import App
from google.adk.plugins import LoggingPlugin
# ... lookup_policy and AuditPlugin from the previous slide

root_agent = Agent(
    name="claims_assistant",
    model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    instruction=("Answer coverage questions. "
                 "Always call lookup_policy first."),
    tools=[lookup_policy],
)

# adk run / web / api_server use a variable named `app` when it exists
app = App(name="claims_api", root_agent=root_agent,
          plugins=[LoggingPlugin(), AuditPlugin()])

The App is what you run and deploy: one agent tree plus its plugins.

root_agent answers coverage questions with one tool.

App takes name, root_agent and plugins. A wrong kwarg raises.

The CLI loads app if it exists. Else it wraps root_agent.

Docs AppsDocs Plugins
Same file, bottom half. Click 1: root_agent is the claims assistant with one tool. Click 2: the App holds the agent and the plugins as one deployable unit. App is a pydantic model that rejects unknown fields, so App(agent=...) fails: the field is root_agent. It has three more config fields (events compaction, context cache, resumability) that later chapters use. Click 3: adk run, adk web and adk api_server share one loader. It imports agent.py through __init__.py ("from . import agent"); if the module has a variable named app it uses that App and its plugins, otherwise it wraps root_agent. Put the .env file with GOOGLE_API_KEY in agents/claims_api/. The audit log is visible in the adk web State tab, or through the session GET two slides later. Analogy: the App is a shipping container: the agent is the cargo, and the plugins travel in the same box. Never pass plugins to the Runner: that is deprecated, and with app= it raises.

Lab 2 Acme claims API · step 3 of 3

POST /run returns the whole turn as a JSON list of events

terminal 2 · labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/rest_calls.sh · excerpt
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/run \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "appName":"claims_api","userId":"u-tom","sessionId":"claim-77",
  "newMessage":{"role":"user","parts":[
    {"text":"What is my collision deductible on POL-448120?"}]}}'

One POST runs one turn of the App in the session you created.

Bodies use camelCase: appName, sessionId. snake_case also works.

The reply arrives once, when the turn ends: tool call, tool result, answer.

The last event holds the text. Read content.parts for it.

Same server, same session claim-77. Click 1: the request names the app, the user and the session; the bodies use camelCase, and snake_case names such as app_name also work because the request model accepts both. Click 2: /run waits for the whole turn and then returns a JSON list of Events: the model's functionCall for lookup_policy, the functionResponse with the deductible, and the final text. The AuditPlugin also ran, so the session now has one audit_log entry; the next-but-one slide reads it. Click 3: the answer is in the last event's content.parts. Analogy: /run is a letter that arrives when the turn is done. A likely question: "Is the response shape stable?" It is the Event model that the Python Runner yields, serialised with camelCase aliases, so the same parsing code works for both.

Repo google/adk-python · cli/api_server.py
Same body as /run, same session claim-77, new question. Click 1: curl -N switches off output buffering, so each line shows the moment the server sends it. Click 2: /run_sse sends one data line per event while the turn runs: the tool call, the tool result, then the answer, three events, and the counter follows them. Click 3: add "streaming": true to the body and the server also sends partial text chunks, so expect more lines; your client must then join the partial text. Analogy: /run is a letter that arrives when the turn is done; /run_sse is a phone call that you hear as it happens. On Windows the single-quoted JSON breaks in PowerShell, so use Git Bash or WSL. A likely question: "Which one does a chat UI use?" /run_sse, because the user sees the tool call and the answer as they happen.

Last call of step 3: GET the session. The response holds the state and the events; this slide shows the state. Click 1: turn 1, the /run call, invoked lookup_policy once, and the AuditPlugin wrote the first audit_log entry before the tool ran. Build Acme claims API · remember the customer

A state prefix decides how long each key lives

python claims/claims_faq.py
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claims_faq.py · excerpt
def get_policy(topic: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    tool_context.state["temp:last_topic"] = topic        # this turn only
    asked = tool_context.state.get("user:topics_asked", [])
    tool_context.state["user:topics_asked"] = asked + [topic]
# ... in main():
s1 = await svc.create_session(
    app_name="claims_api", user_id="u-tom",
    state={"app:company_name": "Acme", "user:customer_name": "Tom"})
async for _ in runner.run_async(
        user_id="u-tom", session_id=s1.id, new_message=msg,
        state_delta={"user:language": "English"}):
    pass

Keys without a prefix live in one chat. A prefix changes the lifetime.

Seed app: and user: keys at create. app: is shared by every user.

Send per-turn context as state_delta. It is written through an event.

temp: lives for this turn. user: follows u-tom into every chat.

Codelab Building Stateful and Personalized Agents with ADK
This build is a standalone FAQ agent, claims_faq_agent, under the same app_name claims_api and the same customer u-tom; the full file is labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claims_faq.py. Start with the four buckets: a key without a prefix belongs to one session, so a new chat starts without it. Click 1: create_session seeds an app: key and a user: key. Warn the room: app: keys are shared by every user of the app, so never write customer data there. Click 2: the state_delta on run_async writes the language through an event, which is the legal way to inject per-turn context such as locale or channel. Click 3: the tool writes temp:last_topic, which lives only for this turn and is trimmed before commit, and appends to user:topics_asked, which follows u-tom into every chat. Analogy: app: is the office noticeboard, user: is the customer file, unprefixed keys are the notepad for this call, and temp: is a sticky note you throw away when you hang up. A likely question: "Where does InMemorySessionService keep user: keys?" In separate app and user dicts that it merges into every session it returns.

Same file, the agent and the second session. Step 0: this is the state after Tom asked about glass in session 1; the temp:last_topic key was trimmed before commit, so it was never stored. Click 1: the instruction reads state with curly-brace templates. The question mark in {user:language?} makes the key optional, so a missing key renders as an empty string; without the question mark a missing key raises a KeyError on the first turn, so seed required keys at create time. Click 2: output_key writes the final answer into last_answer, which has no prefix, so it belongs to this chat only. Click 3: create a second session for the same user: it starts with the app: and user: keys and nothing else. The in-memory service keeps these only while the process runs; the next slide moves sessions into a SQLite file. Analogy: a new call opens the same customer file, with a clean notepad. A likely question: "Can I read user: keys before any session exists?" Yes, with get_user_state on services that support it.

    SqliteSessionService)
# ...
app = App(name="claims_api", root_agent=claims_followup)

Before: the session is a dict in process memory. Run 2 starts empty.

Import the service from its module. No extra install: aiosqlite is core.

Run 1 writes its 2 events to claims_sessions.db in the current folder.

Run 2 is a new process. It loads claim-77 from the file and answers.

Same app name claims_api, same user u-tom, same session claim-77 as in Lab 2 step 3. Step 0, the before block: InMemoryRunner keeps the session in a Python dict, so when the first process exits the conversation goes with it, and the second process answers that it does not have that detail. Click 1: the fix swaps the session service. Import SqliteSessionService from google.adk.sessions.sqlite_session_service, because it is not re-exported; it needs no extra install, because aiosqlite is a core dependency. Click 2: one constructor with a file name; the file is created in the current folder, and you delete it to start fresh. The first run stores 2 events, the user message and the reply. Click 3: the Runner takes session_service=sessions and auto_create_session=True; run 2 is a new process that loads claim-77 from the file, answers with the 2024 Civic, and the count goes to 4. Analogy: the in-memory runner is a whiteboard that is wiped when the meeting ends; SQLite is the claim folder in the filing cabinet. For production, install google-adk[db] and asyncpg and use DatabaseSessionService with a postgresql+asyncpg URL; only ADK 1.28 and later can read sessions that 2.x writes, so upgrade every reader first.
Build Acme claims API · sessions that survive a restart

Seed claim_id once, then every run appends to the same file

labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claims_followup.py · excerpt
async def main(text: str) -> None:
    # ... runner = Runner(app=app, session_service=sessions, ...)
    sid, uid = "claim-77", "u-tom"
    old = await sessions.get_session(app_name="claims_api",
                                     user_id=uid, session_id=sid)
    delta = None if old else {"claim_id": sid}  # seed once
    msg = types.UserContent(parts=[types.Part(text=text)])
    async for ev in runner.run_async(
            user_id=uid, session_id=sid,
            new_message=msg, state_delta=delta):
        if ev.is_final_response() and ev.content and ev.content.parts:
            print(f"[{ev.author}] {ev.content.parts[0].text}")
    s = await sessions.get_session(app_name="claims_api",
                                   user_id=uid, session_id=sid)
    print(f"(events stored: {len(s.events)})")

Run the script twice, as two processes. Both open the same file.

Process 1 stores 2 events: the message and the reply.

Process 2 loads them, answers, and adds 2 more.

The main function of claims_followup.py, run as two separate processes. Click 1: get_session tells first contact from a returning session; the script seeds claim_id only on first contact, because a delta on every run would write the same value in a new event each turn. The same id is stored as claim_id, so there is one key for the claim. Click 2: process 1 sends "My car is a 2024 Civic." and stores 2 events, the user message and the reply. Click 3: process 2 asks "Which car did I say I have?"; it loads claim-77 from the file, answers with the Civic, and the count goes to 4. Analogy: each run adds two pages to the same claim folder. A likely question: "Can adk web open this file?" Yes: adk web --session_service_uri sqlite:///claims_sessions.db opens the same store.
Gotcha Structured output

output_key drops None fields, so read optional keys with .get()

SymptomKeyError: 'incident_date' in the downstream claims code. Causeoutput_key stores model_dump(exclude_none=True). Null fields vanish. FixRead with .get(), or rebuild the typed object.
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claim_intake.py · excerpt
claim = s.state["claim"]            # a dict, None fields dropped
# ...
date = claim.get("incident_date")   # None, not KeyError
typed = ClaimIntake.model_validate(claim)   # typed object back

Symptom first: the downstream claims code crashes with KeyError 'incident_date'. Click 1, the cause: the email in Lab 2 had no year, so the model returned null; with output_key and output_schema, ADK stores model_dump with exclude_none=True, so a null field is not stored as None, it is absent from the dict. Click 2, the fix: read optional keys with .get, which returns None. Click 3: or rebuild the typed object with ClaimIntake.model_validate, which fills the default None again and gives you attribute access. Analogy: the claim form has no box for a missing date, so the clerk leaves the box out instead of writing "none". A likely question: "Can I turn exclude_none off?" Not through output_key; if you need every key, validate the dict back into the model as shown.
Gotcha Structured output

Put the schema on the agent, not in generate_content_config

SymptomResponse schema must be set via LlmAgent.output_schema, not via generate_content_config.response_schema. CauseAn old google-genai habit: the schema went into GenerateContentConfig. FixSet output_schema=ClaimIntake on the agent. ADK validates the reply for you.
wrong place
Agent(name="claim_intake", ...,
  generate_content_config=
    GenerateContentConfig(
      response_schema=))
×
right place
Agent(name="claim_intake", ...,
  output_schema=,
  output_key="claim")
✓
ClaimIntake

ADK raises the error above. No claim reaches state.

ADK owns the schema, so it rejects a second copy in the model config.

Move the schema to output_schema. Add output_key to store the result.

With tools on an AI Studio key, traces show an extra set_model_response call. That is expected.

Second structured-output mistake. Step 0: ADK raises an error whose full text ends with "Move your schema to LlmAgent(output_schema=...)". Click 1: the cause is an old google-genai habit of putting response_schema into GenerateContentConfig; ADK manages the schema itself, so it rejects it there. Click 2: the schema belongs on the agent as output_schema, and output_key stores the validated result in state. Click 3, a likely question: "Why does my trace show an extra set_model_response call when I add tools?" On an AI Studio key ADK cannot combine a schema and tools natively, so it adds a set_model_response tool and asks the model to answer through it. With GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE=1, the Agent Platform backend formerly called Vertex AI, the call goes away. On AI Studio it still works; there is nothing to fix. A related error: Agent(temperature=0) also fails; put temperature in generate_content_config instead.
Gotcha Session state

get_session returns a copy, so write state through an event

SymptomYou set claim_status. The next get_session does not show it. Causeget_session returns a detached copy. Edits on it never reach the store. FixWrite through state_delta=, tool_context.state or callback_context.state.
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/mark_reviewed.py · excerpt
key = dict(app_name="claims_api", user_id="u-tom",
           session_id="claim-77")
s = await sessions.get_session(**key)
s.state["claim_status"] = "reviewed"         # edits the copy: lost
# ...

    parts=[types.Part(text="Mark the claim reviewed.")])

        user_id="u-tom", session_id="claim-77", new_message=msg,
        state_delta={"claim_status": "reviewed"}):
    pass                     # the delta rides on this turn
s = await sessions.get_session(**key)
print("after state_delta:", s.state["claim_status"])

Repo in_memory_session_service.py
This is the same claim-77 session from the SQLite slides; the script is labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/mark_reviewed.py. Step 0: someone marks the claim reviewed, and the next read does not show it. Click 1: get_session returns a detached object. The in-memory service deep-copies the session, and the SQLite and Postgres services build a new object from the rows, so editing s.state changes only your copy. Click 2: state changes persist only when they travel inside an event: state_delta on run_async, tool_context.state in a tool, or callback_context.state in a callback. Here state_delta rides on a normal user turn, so the agent also replies. Click 3: read the session again and the value is there, because the event wrote it to claims_sessions.db. Analogy: get_session is a photocopy of the claim file; writing on the photocopy does not change the file in the cabinet. A likely question: "Can I write state without running the agent?" Not with these public calls; in this course every write goes through a turn, a tool or a callback.
arXiv Aug 2026

Schema text is a second prompt, so put the reasoning field first

arXiv 2608.08254 2026-08-08

Your Prompt Is Not the Only Prompt: How Much Do LLMs Weight Structured-Output Schema Descriptions?

Conflicting schema descriptions cut accuracy by 5-45 pts. Claude Haiku 4.5 fell from 52.5% to 7%.
A required reasoning field before the label: +15-24 pts schema-only accuracy.
Keep the instruction and the Field text consistent. Keep reasoning first.
arXiv 2608.08254

severity "high = injury or > $10k"
reasoning "one sentence"+15-24 pts
order: label first
LLMreads both
Conflicting schema textClaude Haiku 4.5 · accuracy
52.5% → 52.5%
Paper slide, August 2026. Step 0: the instruction and the output_schema both reach the model, and this schema starts with the label fields. Click 1: make the two texts conflict: the instruction says high means injury only, and the Field description says high means a loss over $10k. The paper measured accuracy drops of 5 to 45 points from conflicts like this; Claude Haiku 4.5 fell from 52.5% to 7%, and the bar shows that drop to scale. Click 2: make the two texts say the same thing and move the reasoning field to the top; a required reasoning field before the label raised schema-only accuracy by 15 to 24 points. Click 3: what to change on Monday: review Field descriptions like prompts, and keep reasoning first. Our Lab 2 ClaimIntake schema already does both. Analogy: the small print on a form is part of the instructions; if it contradicts the cover letter, people follow the small print. A likely question: "Does the field order matter to pydantic?" Not to pydantic, but the model writes the fields in order, so the reasoning is written before the label.

Valid JSON is not correct JSON, so check meaning in code

arXiv 2609.23742 2026-09-20

Constrained Decoding Eliminates Structural Failures in Small LLMs but Reveals a Scale-Dependent Semantic Gap

Schema validity went from 78.6-92.9% to 100%.
Semantic errors remained, and the gap depends on model scale.
Add a deterministic meaning check after the extraction.
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/claims/claim_intake.py · excerpt
def check_claim(claim: dict) -> None:
    big_loss = claim.get("estimated_loss_usd", 0) > 10_000
    hurt = claim.get("injuries_reported", False)
    if claim["severity"] == "high" and not (hurt or big_loss):
        raise ValueError("severity=high needs injury or > $10k loss")

Paper slide, September 2026. Click 1: constrained decoding forces the model to emit tokens that fit the schema, and schema validity in small models went from 78.6-92.9% to 100%. The bar shows the band and the jump. Click 2: but the meaning can still be wrong, and the paper finds that this semantic gap depends on model scale. Our example: a valid "high" with no injury and a $6,400 loss passes the schema and is still wrong. Click 3: what to change on Monday: check_claim runs in your code right after get_session and raises ValueError when severity is high without an injury or a loss over $10k; it is in claim_intake.py in the lab folder. Analogy: a form with a box for each answer still lets you write the wrong answer in the right box. A likely question: "Does output_schema not validate this already?" It validates types and enum values, not business rules, so the business rule lives in your code.
Best practices Acme claims API · typed outputs

Typed outputs: four rules to check in every code review

  • Put reasoning first in output_schema: +15-24 pts.
  • Check meaning in code: valid JSON is not correct JSON.
  • Read optional keys with .get(): None fields are dropped.
  • Never set response_schema in generate_content_config.
arXiv 2608.08254arXiv 2609.23742
The chapter as rules you can test in code review, in four clicks; this slide covers typed outputs. Click 1: keep the reasoning field first, because arXiv 2608.08254 measured +15 to 24 points for it, and keep the Field descriptions consistent with the instruction. Click 2: check meaning in code after the extraction, because constrained decoding gives valid JSON that can still carry a wrong severity (arXiv 2609.23742); check_claim in the lab is the pattern. Click 3: read optional keys with .get, because output_key drops null fields such as incident_date. Click 4: never put response_schema into generate_content_config: ADK raises and tells you to use output_schema. Analogy: these are the four boxes a reviewer ticks on every schema pull request. A likely question: "Should every field have a description?" Yes, but review it like a prompt, because the model reads it as one.
Best practices Acme claims API · scoped state

Scoped state: pick the prefix by lifetime, write through events

  • Pick the prefix by lifetime: app:, user:, no prefix, temp:.
  • Write through state_delta, tools or callbacks, not a copy.
  • Use a business key as session id: retries join one chat.
  • Never store secrets in state: adk web and the GET route show them.
Docs State
Rules for state, one click each. Click 1: pick the prefix by lifetime: app: for tenant config shared by every user, user: for the customer, no prefix for this chat, temp: for scratch values that die with the turn. Click 2: write state only through events: state_delta on run_async, tool_context.state in a tool, or callback_context.state in a callback; an edit on the object that get_session returns is lost, because it is a copy. Click 3: use a business key such as claim-77 as the session id, as we did on the REST and SQLite slides, so a retry or a channel switch joins the same chat and support staff can find it. Click 4: never put secrets in state, because adk web and GET /apps/.../sessions/... show it to anyone who can call them. Analogy: state is the claim folder: anything in it can be photocopied by whoever opens it. A likely question: "Where do API keys go then?" In environment variables or a secret manager that your tools read.
Best practices Acme claims API · one App per folder

One App per folder: name it like the folder, plugins on the App

  • Name the App like its folder, with underscores: claims_api.
  • Register plugins on the App: every agent gets them.
  • Never pass plugins= to Runner: with app= it raises.
Docs Apps
labs/adk/lab2-claims-api/agents/run_claims.py · excerpt
from claims_api.agent import app      # the one App, plugins included

async def main() -> None:
    sessions = SqliteSessionService(db_path="claims_sessions.db")
    runner = Runner(app=app, session_service=sessions,
                    auto_create_session=True)      # no plugins= here
Rules for the deployable unit. Click 1: name the App like its folder, because the server names each app after its folder; the folder name must be a valid Python identifier, so use underscores, not hyphens. run_claims.py imports the one App from claims_api.agent instead of building a second one; run it from the agents folder. Click 2: register plugins on the App, so every agent in the tree gets the audit and logging hooks, in adk run, adk web, adk api_server and your own Runner alike. Click 3: never pass plugins to the Runner: that argument is deprecated with the warning "The plugins argument is deprecated. Please use the app argument to provide plugins instead.", and together with app= it raises. Analogy: one building, one security desk, one address on the door. A likely question: "Can one folder hold two Apps?" The loader takes the variable named app, so keep one App per folder and split other agents into their own folders.

Workflow graphs

Build the Acme support desk as a graph: a typed chain, a router, and the same router in YAML.

"The graph model is worth the learning curve as soon as you have more than two branching paths."

Docs Google Cloud, I/O '26 news for agent developers (2026-05-19) Acme support desk tested on google-adk 2.13.0
This chapter builds the Acme support desk as three graphs; press three times to preview them. Step 1 is the refund chain: parse the request, check the 30-day policy, write the reply, write an audit line, always in that order. Step 2 is the triage router: the model labels the ticket from a closed set, and a plain function picks the route, so a P1 outage always pages on-call. Step 3 is the same router as YAML that a PM or a lawyer can review. After the lab: porting a 1.x SequentialAgent, two gotchas (a silent route failure and two loud graph errors), one paper on what routing costs, and a rules slide. Think of the graph as the rail track and the model as the driver: the driver sets the speed, but the track decides where the train can go. A likely question: "When do I need a graph instead of one agent with tools?" Google's I/O '26 advice is the quote on the slide: as soon as you have more than two branching paths.
