Step 2 of Lab 5A opens manager_gate. Three clicks. First, the limit: a $320 refund would route straight to issue_refund, which the dashed token shows; nobody is asked. Second, the id: iid is built from invocation_id and run_id, and on the first run resume_inputs.get(iid) returns None, because nobody has answered yet. Third, the question: the node yields a RequestInput with that id, the ManagerDecision schema, and a payload with the amount and the draft, so the approval screen shows exactly what is approved. The run pauses; on the wire this is a FunctionCall named adk_request_input whose id is the interrupt id, and it is listed in event.long_running_tool_ids. Think of the interrupt id as a ticket number stapled to the form: when the form comes back, the clerk finds the answer under that number. A likely question: "Why build the id by hand and not let ADK make one?" The default is a new uuid, and on a rerun that would never match the stored answer; the gotcha slides come back to this. Next: the same function runs again and finds the answer.
Lab 5A Acme refund approvals · step 3 of 5

On the rerun, the same id finds the answer and picks one route

labs/adk/lab5a-refund-approval/refund_approval/agent.py · excerpt
class ManagerDecision(BaseModel):
  approved: bool
  amount: Optional[float] = None          # partial refund
  note: str = ""
# ... manager_gate, run 2 (rerun_on_resume=True):
  answer = ctx.resume_inputs.get(iid)     # None on the first run
  # ... (the "if answer is None" branch is skipped)
  d = ManagerDecision.model_validate(answer)
  if not d.approved:
    yield Event(route="rejected")
  elif d.note:
    yield Event(state={"note": d.note}, route="revise")
  else:
    yield Event(state={"final_amount": d.amount or amount},
                route="approved")

The reply must fit this schema.

A JSON object such as {"approved": true} fits it.

The function runs again from the top. Now get(iid) returns the reply.

One route fires: approved, rejected or revise.

A note means revise: a new pass, a new run_id, a new id.

Step 3 of Lab 5A is the second half of manager_gate. ManagerDecision is the reply schema: approved is required, amount allows a partial refund, and note asks for a new draft. Because the decorator says rerun_on_resume=True, the whole function runs again from the top after the reply, and this time resume_inputs.get(iid) finds the answer, since invocation_id and run_id are the same on a resume. With the default rerun_on_resume=False, the hand-off pattern, the reply itself becomes the node output and the next node must read it; Lab 5B uses that pattern. model_validate turns the reply into a ManagerDecision, and exactly one route fires. The revise route goes back to draft_reply inside the same invocation, so the gate runs again with run_id 2 and asks with a new id ending in _2. Think of a revise as a new form with a new ticket number, so an old answer can never approve a new draft. A likely question: "What if the manager types approve, not JSON?" model_validate raises a ValidationError; step 5 shows why.

Each reply finds its pause by the saved interrupt id.

This is the same refund_approval agent, run as three separate processes against one session. Monday at 10:00 the customer asks for 820 dollars, the gate pauses, adk run saves the session in SQLite under refund_approval/.adk and exits with code 2, so a script can tell "paused" from "done". On Tuesday the manager answers from a brand-new process: adk run sees the open interrupt in the session and sends the reply as a FunctionResponse with the interrupt id, printing "Auto-resuming interrupt". The note routes to revise, draft_reply writes a new draft, and the gate pauses again with a new id ending in _2, because a revise pass is a new run of the node. The third process approves 700 dollars, a partial refund, and issue_refund prints the idempotency key refund-A-2040. The last click shows the link between processes: each reply is matched to the saved interrupt by its id. Think of the session as a case folder on a shelf: any clerk on any day can pick it up and continue. A likely question: "Do I need ResumabilityConfig for this?" No: answering a pause is a new turn, and the Runner finds the paused run from the response id; ResumabilityConfig is for continuing a crashed run, in Lab 5B.

Replies are JSON-parsed, so only a JSON object fits the schema

manager typesapprove42true{"approved": true}

the same JSON reply in three shells
# bash, zsh
$ adk run refund_approval '{"approved": true}' --session_id case-2040
# Windows cmd
$ adk run refund_approval "{\"approved\": true}" --session_id case-2040
# Windows PowerShell 5.1

Answering a pause is a new turn. It needs no ResumabilityConfig.

Step 5 closes Lab 5A with the type trap. adk run sends every reply as {"result": text}, and the engine JSON-parses string results when it can. So the word approve stays a str, 42 becomes an int, and true becomes a bool, and ManagerDecision.model_validate rejects all three with a ValidationError. Only a JSON object becomes a dict, and only a dict becomes a ManagerDecision. The docs say response_schema "does not reshape the reply": the reply must already be in that format. The last click shows the quoting for each shell: cmd needs the inner quotes escaped, and Windows PowerShell 5.1 needs the escaped form inside single quotes. It also separates two ideas people mix up: answering a HITL pause is a new turn and works from adk run with no ResumabilityConfig; ResumabilityConfig is for continuing an interrupted or crashed invocation from your own Runner code, which Lab 5B shows. Think of the schema as a form with boxes: a sticky note that says "approve" does not fill the boxes. A likely question: "Can I accept plain text anyway?" Yes, parse the str yourself; the HITL gotcha slide shows how.

Lab 5B is the Acme payout desk, and it needs no API key because there is no LLM node. Install google-adk 2.13.0 and run every command from labs/adk/lab5b-payouts-durable. Walk the four focus steps. kyc_lookup appends one line to side_effects.log; that line is our proof later that a finished node is replayed, not run again. analyst_review is a plain function that yields a RequestInput, so ADK wraps it as a function node with the default hand-off pattern: the analyst's reply becomes its output, and that output is the node_input of pay. The edges chain the three nodes. Last, the App turns on ResumabilityConfig and the Runner keeps the session in payouts.db with SqliteSessionService, so a second process can read it. Think of side_effects.log as the stamp on a parcel: if a parcel has two stamps, somebody sent it twice. A likely question: "Why a file and not a print?" A print goes away with the process; the file survives the restart and lets you count real executions.
Lab 5B Acme payouts · step 2 of 6

RetryConfig retries the gateway 503 with exact 0.5 s and 1.0 s waits

labs/adk/lab5b-payouts-durable/payouts/app.py · excerpt
@node(retry_config=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4, initial_delay=0.5,
                               backoff_factor=2.0, jitter=0.0,
                               exceptions=[ConnectionError,
                                           "NodeTimeoutError"]),
      timeout=2.0)
async def pay(ctx: Context, node_input: str):  # the analyst's reply
  yield Event(message=f"gateway attempt {ctx.attempt_count}")
  if node_input.strip().lower() != "yes":
    yield Event(output="CANCELLED"); return
  if ctx.attempt_count < 3:
    raise ConnectionError("gateway 503")   # attempts 1-2 fail, 3 pays
  key = "payout-" + ctx.invocation_id      # same key on every run
  yield Event(output=f"PAID idempotency_key={key}")
output · illustrative
[payouts] gateway attempt 1
[payouts] gateway attempt 2
[payouts] gateway attempt 3
OUTPUT: PAID idempotency_key=payout-e-9c1…
Step 2 of Lab 5B is the pay node. Walk the RetryConfig line first: max_attempts counts the first try, so 4 means one try and up to three retries, and with jitter at zero the waits are exact: 0.5 seconds and then 1.0 second, because the delay is initial_delay times backoff_factor to the power attempt minus one. The node fails twice with a gateway 503 and pays on attempt 3, which ctx.attempt_count shows; the fourth slot stays unused. The last click is the idempotency key: payout- plus the invocation id, the same value on every retry and every resume, so the gateway can drop a duplicate charge. The output needs the driver main(), which the next slides build. Think of backoff as a polite caller: wait a little, then a little longer, so a busy line has time to clear. A likely question: "Is the attempt counter saved?" No: after an interrupt or a restart the node gets its full retry budget back.

With jitter=0.0 every wait is exact. Use it in tests.

The defaults add jitter. Keep it in production to spread load.

This build slide hardens the pay node from step 2. The exceptions list matches exception class names along the MRO. A timeout raises NodeTimeoutError, which is not a ConnectionError, so with only ConnectionError in the list a 2-second timeout ends the node on attempt 1; the error text is "Node 'pay' timed out after 2.0 seconds." Add the string "NodeTimeoutError" and the timeout is retried like the 503. The right side is about jitter. Our lab sets jitter=0.0, so the wait before try 2 is exactly 0.5 seconds every time, which is what you want in a test. RetryConfig() with no arguments resolves to max_attempts=5, initial_delay=1.0, max_delay=60, backoff_factor=2.0 and jitter=1.0, so the wait before try 2 lands anywhere between 0 and 2 seconds; keep jitter on in production to spread load. Think of jitter as staggering the start times of runners so they do not all hit the gateway at the same second. A likely question: "Why a string and not the class?" Both match by name; the string saves an import of an internal error class.

    msg = types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part(text=arg)])

                                   invocation_id=inv, new_message=msg):
    if ev.long_running_tool_ids:              # analyst_review paused
      json.dump({"invocation_id": ev.invocation_id,
                 "interrupt_id": next(iter(ev.long_running_tool_ids))},
                open("pending.json", "w"))

Step 4 of Lab 5B is the first half of the driver, main(). Process 1 is "start": it creates the session s1 in payouts.db and sends the payee name as the first message. run_async streams events; kyc_lookup runs and writes its one log line, then analyst_review yields a RequestInput. That event carries long_running_tool_ids, which is how a driver sees a pause. The driver writes the invocation id and the interrupt id to pending.json and the loop ends, so the interpreter exits with nothing left in memory. Everything the next process needs is now on disk: the session in SQLite and the two ids in a small file. Think of pending.json as the claim ticket you get when you leave a coat: the coat stays in the building, you keep only the number. A likely question: "Why save the invocation id too?" The resume call passes it so the Runner continues that invocation; the interrupt id alone names the question, not the run. For a fresh run, delete payouts.db, pending.json and side_effects.log, because start creates s1 again.

Docs adk.dev Resume
The last step of Lab 5B is the crash case. Try it: press Ctrl-C during attempt 2 of "resume yes", then run "python -m payouts.app continue -". The continue branch passes only the invocation id and no new message; the Runner then continues the interrupted invocation from the checkpoint events in payouts.db. That works only because the App sets ResumabilityConfig(is_resumable=True); without it, the same call fails with "ValueError: Running an agent requires a new_message or a resumable app." kyc_lookup replays and the log still has one line, and the attempt counter starts again, so pay gets its full retry budget back. The table separates the two kinds of resume that people mix up. Answering a pause sends a FunctionResponse, needs no ResumabilityConfig, and works from adk run and adk web. Continuing after a crash sends no message, needs ResumabilityConfig and your own Runner: the docs say resuming from the ADK Web UI or the CLI is not supported. Think of the checkpoint as the bookmark from the chapter opener: you go back to the page you were on, and you read that page again. A likely question: "Then why do I still need an idempotency key?" Because resume is at-least-once: a crash between the charge and the saved event re-runs pay; the retry gotcha comes back to this.
Build

Swap the hand-written gate for one require_confirmation decorator

labs/adk/lab5a-refund-approval/refund_confirm/agent.py · excerpt
AUTO_APPROVE_LIMIT = 500.0
def intake(node_input: str):     # "A-2040 820"
  order_id, amount = node_input.split()[:2]
  yield Event(state={"order_id": order_id, "amount": float(amount)})
# The predicate gets `amount` by name from state. Return a real bool.
@node(require_confirmation=lambda amount: amount > AUTO_APPROVE_LIMIT)
def issue_refund(order_id: str, amount: float):  # args = state keys
  key = f"refund-{order_id}"                     # idempotency key
  yield Event(message=f"REFUNDED ${amount:.2f} on {order_id} "
                      f"(key {key})")
root_agent = Workflow(name="refund_confirm",
                      edges=[("START", intake, issue_refund)])
Trade-off: yes or no only. No draft, no revise loop, no partial amount.
This build slide replaces the hand-written manager_gate from Lab 5A with one decorator on issue_refund. The first click collapses the gate node into a pause badge on issue_refund: the graph is now START, intake, issue_refund. The second click is the predicate: lambda amount: amount > AUTO_APPROVE_LIMIT uses the same 500-dollar constant as the old gate, and amount is bound by name from the state key that intake wrote; for 820 it returns True, so the node pauses before its body runs. The third click is the honest part: the line count drops from 19 to one decorator because the decorator is a yes/no gate. The draft, the revise loop and the partial amount go away, so keep the RequestInput gate with ManagerDecision when a manager approves 700 instead of 820 or adds a note. It is like a door with a built-in badge reader instead of a guard who stands in front of it. This needs google-adk 2.12 or newer; the lab is tested against 2.13.0 source. A likely question: "Can the predicate see other state?" It gets the node's bound args by name, plus ctx, node_input and any state key with a matching name. Next: what the reply must look like.

$ adk run refund_confirm "A-2040 820" --session_id case-2040
$ adk run refund_confirm '{"confirmed": true}' --session_id case-2040

The pause is a RequestInput with id wf_tool_confirmation:<node_path>

manager repliesnode getsresult · illustrative
{"confirmed": true}ToolConfirmationREFUNDED $820.00 on A-2040 (key refund-A-2040)
{"confirmed": false}ToolConfirmationbody skipped · {"error": "This tool call is rejected."}
yesstrWorkflowDataError: A tool confirmation response must be a ToolConfirmation payload, but got str.
Now run the decorated node from the same lab folder. The first command pauses: node confirmation is a RequestInput whose interrupt id is wf_tool_confirmation plus the node path and whose schema is ToolConfirmation. The second command answers it. Because adk run JSON-parses the reply text, you type the JSON object as the query: {"confirmed": true} becomes a dict, the node body runs once, and the refund line comes out with its idempotency key. {"confirmed": false} is a rejection: the body does not run, and the node output is {"error": "This tool call is rejected."}. A plain yes stays a string, and the node raises WorkflowDataError with the exact text on the slide. Think of the badge reader again: it reads only badges, so a spoken "yes" at the door does nothing. A likely question: "Can I make yes work?" Not with the decorator; put a small normalizer node before it, or keep the RequestInput gate and parse the string yourself. Gotcha Human-in-the-loop · 1 of 3

A uuid4 interrupt id changes on every rerun, so the gate asks forever

SymptomThe manager answers. The node asks again. CauseA new id on each rerun. The lookup never matches. FixBuild the id from invocation_id + run_id.
refund_approval/agent.py · manager_gate
# not: iid = str(uuid4())
iid = f"refund_approval_{ctx.invocation_id}_{ctx.run_id}"
answer = ctx.resume_inputs.get(iid)   # found on the rerun
The first HITL bug hits the Acme refund gate after the lab works on your laptop. A rerun_on_resume node runs again after every reply, so its interrupt id must be the same on every rerun. With uuid4 the id changes each time: the answer is stored under the old id, resume_inputs.get looks under the new one, misses, and the node asks the manager again. The animation counts it: the top row asks again and again, the bottom row asks once and hits. The fix is the lab's own line: build the id from invocation_id and run_id, which stay the same on a resume and change only on a new revise pass. Think of the interrupt id as a cloakroom ticket: if you print a new ticket every time you come back, you never get your coat. A likely question: "Why not reuse one fixed string?" Reuse is supported, but the RequestInput docstring still recommends unique ids per loop pass, which the revise loop needs.
Gotcha Human-in-the-loop · 2 of 3

The manager types approve, and model_validate raises ValidationError

SymptomValidationError when the manager types approve. CauseThe reply stays a str. response_schema does not reshape it. FixAccept a str and parse it yourself. LimitNotes and partial amounts still need JSON.
refund_approval/agent.py · manager_gate
answer = ctx.resume_inputs.get(iid)   # the manager typed: approve
d = ManagerDecision.model_validate(answer)
# pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error
# for ManagerDecision
refund_approval/agent.py · manager_gate
answer = ctx.resume_inputs.get(iid)
if isinstance(answer, str):           # "approve" stays a str
  # approve/reject only: anything else is a reject
  answer = {"approved": answer.strip().lower() == "approve"}
d = ManagerDecision.model_validate(answer)
The second HITL bug is the type trap from Lab 5A step 5, now in production. The CLI and most UIs send the reply as text, and the engine JSON-parses it when it can, so the word approve stays a string and ManagerDecision.model_validate raises a pydantic ValidationError. The docs are explicit: response_schema "does not reshape the reply"; the reply must already be in that format. The fix is to accept a string and turn it into the schema yourself, before model_validate. Be honest about the limit: this small parser covers approve and reject only, anything else becomes a reject, and it loses notes and partial amounts, so ask for JSON when you need those, or put a small LLM normalizer node after the pause. Think of it as a paper form with tick boxes: if someone writes "approve" across the top, a clerk must tick the box for them. A likely question: "Why not make every field optional?" Then a typo would approve nothing and still pass validation; a strict schema plus an explicit parser keeps the decision visible.
Gotcha Human-in-the-loop · 3 of 3 · open #7010

A predicate that returns None lets an $820 refund run with no prompt

SymptomAn $820 refund runs with no prompt. CauseNo return, so Python returns None. cast(bool, …) does nothing at run time. FixReturn a real bool on every path.
Repo adk-python #7010 Docs adk.dev Human input
refund_approval/agent.py · tool-level FunctionTool
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool
def needs_ok(amount: float, **_) -> bool:  # **_ takes the other args
  amount > AUTO_APPROVE_LIMIT              # no return: None
FunctionTool(issue_refund, require_confirmation=needs_ok)
refund_approval/agent.py · write @node predicates the same way
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool
def needs_ok(amount: float, **_) -> bool:
  if amount > AUTO_APPROVE_LIMIT:
    return True
  return False                             # never fall through
FunctionTool(issue_refund, require_confirmation=needs_ok)
The third HITL bug is issue 7010, still open, about the tool-level FunctionTool predicate. ADK uses cast(bool, ...), which does nothing at run time, so a predicate that forgets its return statement returns None; None is falsy, and an 820-dollar refund runs with no prompt and no error. The fix is boring and strict: return a real bool on every path, and never fall through to the end of the function. Write the predicate of the node-level decorator from the build slide the same way. The double-star underscore parameter takes the other tool arguments, so the predicate only names the one it needs; FunctionTool passes the tool's own arguments to the predicate, so the name amount must match the tool's parameter name. Think of a door alarm with a loose wire: it does not ring, and silence looks exactly like "all clear". A likely question: "How do I catch this in CI?" Add a unit test that calls the predicate with 820 and asserts it is True, and one with 320 that asserts it is False; an assert on the type catches None.
Gotcha Retry and resume · 1 of 3

A node that catches Exception hides the 503, so RetryConfig never retries

SymptomA gateway 503 ends pay on attempt 1. Causeexcept Exception turns the error into a normal output. FixLet transient errors raise. NeverCatch BaseException. ADK interrupts a node with one.
payouts/app.py · pay
async def pay(ctx: Context, node_input: str):
  try:
    if ctx.attempt_count < 3:
      raise ConnectionError("gateway 503")
  except Exception:
    yield Event(output="error"); return  # RetryConfig sees no error
labs/adk/lab5b-payouts-durable/payouts/app.py · pay
  if ctx.attempt_count < 3:
    raise ConnectionError("gateway 503")   # attempts 1-2 fail, 3 pays
  # NodeInterruptedError is a BaseException "so user code
  # cannot accidentally catch it with except Exception".
  # Do not catch BaseException either.
These three bugs hit the ACME-GmbH payout after the retry lab works. The first: a node body that catches Exception and returns "error" turns the 503 into a normal output, so RetryConfig sees a successful node and the payout ends on attempt 1. The 2.0 migration guide says not to wrap node bodies in except Exception for exactly this reason. Let transient errors raise; the retry config decides what to retry. The last click is the stronger rule: never catch BaseException. ADK raises NodeInterruptedError, a BaseException, to interrupt a node, and the source says it does so "so user code cannot accidentally catch it with except Exception". A bare except or except BaseException would swallow the interrupt too. Think of a smoke alarm with a pillow on it: the fire is still there, only the alarm is quiet. A likely question: "Where do I log the error then?" Log and re-raise, or use a plugin or callback; do not return a value from the except block.
Gotcha Retry and resume · 2 of 3 · open #7524

A retry on the whole workflow re-runs a finished sibling: two emails

Symptomsend_email runs again when its sibling retries. CauseThe retry sits on the parent workflow. SQLite only. FixPut retry_config on the node that fails.
Repo adk-python #7524
output · issue #7524 repro · SQLite session
node executions: {'flaky': 2, 'send_email': 2}
emails sent: ['email #1', 'email #2']
The second retry bug is issue 7524, still open. The reporter's graph fans out two nodes, flaky and send_email, under a workflow that carries the retry_config. When flaky fails once on a SQLite session, the workflow retry re-runs the finished send_email too, so the customer gets two emails; a retry on the flaky node itself sends one. The cause is a race: the finished sibling's output was still being persisted when the batch was cancelled, which is why InMemorySessionService passes and SQLite fails. So test retry and resume on the session backend you use in production, not only in memory. Our payout already follows the fix, because the retry sits on pay and nowhere else. Think of a group order: if one dish is wrong, you re-cook that dish, not the whole table's order. A likely question: "Is the workflow-level retry ever right?" Only when every child is idempotent; until the issue is fixed, keep retries on leaf nodes.
Gotcha Retry and resume · 3 of 3

Resume is at-least-once, so a uuid4 key lets the gateway pay twice

SymptomACME-GmbH is paid twice after a crash. CauseA crash after the charge re-runs pay with a new key. FixSend one stable key: "payout-" + invocation_id.
"Tool call to resume needs to be idempotent."
Repo ResumabilityConfig docstring · v2.13.0
payouts/app.py · pay
from uuid import uuid4
async def pay(ctx: Context, node_input: str):
  key = str(uuid4())            # a new key after every resume
  yield Event(output=f"PAID idempotency_key={key}")
labs/adk/lab5b-payouts-durable/payouts/app.py · pay
  key = "payout-" + ctx.invocation_id      # same key on every run
  yield Event(output=f"PAID idempotency_key={key}")
The third retry bug is the expensive one. Resume is at-least-once: if the process crashes after the gateway charged the card but before the node's event was saved, the resumed run executes pay again. With a uuid4 key, the second charge carries a new key, so the gateway cannot tell it is a repeat and ACME-GmbH is paid twice. With payout- plus the invocation id, every retry and every resume of the same run sends the same key, and the gateway drops the duplicate. The ResumabilityConfig docstring says it plainly: "Tool call to resume needs to be idempotent." Think of the idempotency key as a cheque number: the bank pays a given cheque number once, however many times it is presented. Two related points for questions: Pub/Sub triggers create a new session for each redelivery, and since 2.12.0 tools can see the trigger delivery id to detect it; and do not change the graph while runs are paused, because checkpoint versioning is still an open item. Next: three recent papers on what an approval must bind.
arXiv Sep-Oct 2026

Scope each yes to one call: reused and standing approvals get abused

arXiv 2609.33910 2026-09-27

When Consent Outlives Context: Residual Authority Replay in Long-Lived Agents

Reused approvals raised attack success by up to 35.1 pp on AgentDojo.
Scope each yes to one interrupt_id. Never cache it in state.
arXiv 2610.22987 2026-10-16

From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents

Model-authored allow-rules covered 56.9% of tests. 47/58 attacks then ran silently.
Approve one call with its exact arguments. No standing rules.
arXiv 2609.33910 arXiv 2610.22987
Two papers from September and October say the same thing: a yes from a human is only as safe as the scope of that yes. The grid is the 2610.22987 result, not an Acme measurement: one tile is one percent of that paper's capability tests for coding agents, and the approval card on the right is our Acme example. First click: residual authority replay reuses an earlier approval for a new action and raises attack success by up to 35.1 percentage points on AgentDojo, a prompt-injection benchmark. So scope each approval to one interrupt_id and never write "approved" into user: state; a second order, A-2041, gets a new interrupt and a new pause. Second click: in From Approval to Abuse, planted repo context got coding agents to request broad allow-rules in 58% of instances; those rules covered 56.9% of capability tests, and once a rule was approved, 47 of 58 runs reached silent malicious completion. Analogy: a signed cheque names the payee and the amount; a blank signed cheque is a standing rule. A likely question: "Does the ADK gate already scope approvals?" Yes, if you keep the lab's id per pass and never copy the yes into state.

The tool must re-check the approved payload, or edited args slip through

arXiv 2610.21063 2026-10-15

Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization

Re-check the approved payload inside the tool before it pays.
refund_approval/agent.py · issue_refund re-checks the approval
def issue_refund(ctx: Context, order_id: str, final_amount: float):
  ok = ctx.state.get("approved")      # manager_gate writes it with the yes
  if ok != {"order_id": order_id, "amount": final_amount}:
    raise PermissionError("refund differs from the approved payload")

Also cap the session sum: two $490 refunds each pass a $500 gate.

arXiv 2610.21063
The third paper, Approve What, Exactly?, audited agent runtimes and found that the arguments changed after approval in 4 of 8 runtimes where binding could be measured; it also found no runtime that produces a third-party-verifiable approval record. Effect binding means the tool checks the exact approved payload again when it runs. Walk the animation: the manager approves A-2040 for 820 dollars; by the time the tool runs, the amount has become 8,200; the payloads differ, so the tool raises PermissionError and nothing is paid. ADK does not do this for you, so write the approved order and amount to state in manager_gate together with the yes, and compare inside issue_refund, as the code shows. The same paper lists threshold splitting: two 490-dollar refunds each stay under the 500-dollar gate, so also keep a running refunded total in state and pause when the session sum passes the limit. Analogy: the bank compares the amount on the cheque with the amount in words before it pays. A likely question: "Is this the same as the idempotency key?" No: the key stops the same payment twice, binding stops a different payment from riding on an old yes. Next: how Temporal makes each call durable.
In production Kyndryl · Temporal

Temporal makes each ADK model call and tool call a retryable Activity

Kyndryl ran ADK agents as HTTP services. One Activity wrapped one A2A request.

The official plugin makes each model call and each tool call its own Activity.

The worker dies during model call 2. History keeps rows 1 and 2.

A new worker replays history. Only the failed call runs again.

"The agentic loop is actually a deterministic sequence of non-deterministic things."
Blog Temporal · Google ADK integration (2026-04-20)
Kyndryl first ran ADK agents as HTTP services and wrapped one A2A JSON-RPC request in each Temporal Activity, so a failure anywhere inside the agent meant redoing the whole agent call; the struck-through strip keeps that v1 design on screen for contrast. The official Temporal plugin moves the agentic loop into the Workflow and makes each LLM call and each tool call its own Activity; when a call fails, Temporal retries that exact call with the same context history and the same inputs. Walk the ladder: two rows complete, the worker crashes during model call 2, and a new worker replays rows 1 and 2 from history and re-runs only the failed row, shown in amber. To make replay deterministic, ADK moved its time and UUID calls behind google.adk.platform.time and uuid; that is the same reason a uuid4 key in your own replayed code breaks deduplication, as the retry gotcha showed. Analogy: a bank statement, where you re-read the rows you already have and only retry the payment that bounced. Kyndryl published no production numbers, so do not quote any. Next: the code that wires the plugin.
In production Kyndryl · Temporal

TemporalModel and activity_as_tool turn each call into an Activity

pip install "temporalio[google-adk]==1.34.0" "google-adk==2.13.0" temporal server start-dev
payout_workflow.py · temporalio 1.34.0 · excerpt
from temporalio.contrib.google_adk_agents import (
    GoogleAdkPlugin, TemporalModel)
from temporalio.contrib.google_adk_agents.workflow import activity_as_tool
# also imported: timedelta, temporalio.workflow, google.adk.Agent
charge_gateway = ...   # stub: your @activity.defn gateway call
plugin = GoogleAdkPlugin()   # the SAME instance for Client and Worker
@workflow.defn
class PayoutAgentWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        pay_tool = activity_as_tool(          # tool call = an Activity
            charge_gateway, start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=60))
        agent = Agent(name="payout_agent", tools=[pay_tool],
                      model=TemporalModel("gemini-3.5-flash"),  # Activity
                      instruction="Use charge_gateway to pay payouts.")
        # ... run the agent, return its final reply
Workflowagent loop
model callTemporalModel
charge_gatewayactivity_as_tool
Replay re-sends charge_gateway with the same inputs. The gateway still needs the payout- key.
This is the payout agent from this chapter, written for Temporal. Install the pinned versions, temporalio 1.34.0 with the google-adk extra and google-adk 2.13.0, and start a local dev server; the Worker needs GOOGLE_API_KEY. First click: the same GoogleAdkPlugin instance goes to the Client and to the Worker, as the Temporal docs show. Second click: activity_as_tool wraps charge_gateway, your own Activity that calls the gateway, so each tool call is a separate, retryable Activity with a 60-second timeout. Third click: TemporalModel wraps the model, so each model call becomes an invoke_model Activity. Fourth click, the lesson: replay re-sends charge_gateway with the same inputs, so neither Temporal nor ResumabilityConfig makes the ACME-GmbH payout idempotent for you; the gateway still needs the payout- key. The integration package is moving: on sdk-python main the module re-exports temporalio.google_adk from the new temporalio-google-adk 0.0.1 package, but 1.34.0 keeps the contrib path on this slide. The docs page is marked pre-release. A likely question: "Do I need Temporal if ADK has ResumabilityConfig?" ResumabilityConfig checkpoints your ADK workflow in one session store; Temporal adds per-call retries and a history that any worker can replay.
06

Tools are the agent's hands, so give it few, narrow and audited ones.

MCP, OpenAPI and tool errors

Build the Acme claims desk: two MCP servers and a REST API behind least privilege, with errors written for the agent.

MCP: a JSON-RPC protocol for tool servers. ADK's McpToolset is the client.

Codelab Getting Started with MCP, ADK and A2A Docs adk.dev MCP tools
This chapter connects the Acme claims desk to three tool sources. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a JSON-RPC protocol that lets an agent list and call tools on a separate server; ADK's McpToolset is the client side. Over stdio the server is a child process that the agent starts, and over streamable HTTP it is a network service that many agents share. The first source is a claims MCP server over stdio, the second a claims-handbook MCP server over streamable HTTP, and the third the claims-status REST API through OpenAPIToolset. The animation shows the rule for the whole chapter: every source offers more tools than the agent needs, so tool_filter drops purge_claim before the model sees it, and a prefix (claims_, handbook_) tells the model which server each tool comes from. Think of a new adjuster on the first day: you give them the keys to the rooms they need, not the master key. We also write tool errors for the agent, because the agent can only act by calling another tool. Everything is tested on Python 3.11+, google-adk 2.13.0 and mcp 2.3.0, and you will run three processes: claims_api on port 8081, handbook_server on port 3000, and adk web. A likely question: "If I filter tools, can the server still be called directly?" Yes, by other MCP clients, so the server keeps its own checks too. The next slide sets up the lab folder.

A likely question: "Why must terminals 1 and 2 start first?" agent.py fetches the spec at import, and the HTTP toolset connects when the agent first runs.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 1 of 4 · server

An MCP 2.x server exposes claim tools over stdio

python claims_agent/claims_server.py < /dev/null
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/claims_server.py · excerpt
import logging, sys
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer
# stdout carries JSON-RPC: log to stderr only
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.INFO)
mcp = MCPServer("claims-server")
CLAIMS = {"CLM-1001": {"status": "open", "amount": 1800.0}}
@mcp.tool()
def get_claim(claim_id: str) -> dict:
    """Return status and amount (USD) for a claim id like CLM-1001."""
    if claim_id not in CLAIMS:
        return {"status": "error",
                "message": f"Unknown claim {claim_id}."}
    return {"status": "ok", "claim_id": claim_id, **CLAIMS[claim_id]}
# ... approve_claim and purge_claim: next slide
if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()  # transport defaults to "stdio"
output · illustrative
$ python claims_agent/claims_server.py < /dev/null
stdout: empty   # only JSON-RPC goes there
stderr: import errors show here first
This is step 1 of the Acme claims desk lab: a small MCP server with claim tools that the agent starts as a child process. The full file is labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/claims_server.py; the slide shows only the lines that carry the idea. Step 1, the import: mcp 2.x renamed FastMCP to MCPServer, so old tutorials fail with an import error. Step 2, logging goes to stderr, because over stdio the stdout pipe carries the JSON-RPC messages and nothing else. Step 3, the tool: the decorator turns the function into an MCP tool, and the docstring and type hints become its schema; an unknown id gives a structured error, not an exception. Step 4, mcp.run() picks stdio by default. Run the server alone with stdin closed: it starts, reads the end of its input and exits, and any import error shows in the terminal. Think of stdout as a phone line that a fax machine uses: if you say one word into it, the fax fails. A likely question: "Do I start this server myself?" No, McpToolset starts it; you run it alone only to check it imports.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 1 of 4 · server rules

The server keeps its own checks: amount limit and admin role

labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/claims_server.py · excerpt
@mcp.tool()
def approve_claim(claim_id: str, approved_amount: float) -> dict:
    """Approve a claim and pay approved_amount USD."""
    claim = CLAIMS.get(claim_id)
    if claim is None or approved_amount > claim["amount"]:  # rule
        return {"status": "error",
                "message": "Unknown claim or amount too high."}
    claim["status"] = "approved"
    return {"status": "ok", "paid": approved_amount}
@mcp.tool()
def purge_claim(claim_id: str) -> dict:
    """Permanently delete a claim record (admin role only)."""
    if os.environ.get("CLAIMS_ROLE") != "admin":  # role check
        return {"status": "error", "message": "Needs the admin role."}
    purged = CLAIMS.pop(claim_id, None) is not None
    return {"status": "ok", "purged": purged}

Step 2 hides purge_claim from the model. Other MCP clients can still call it.

The server keeps its own rules, whatever the client does. Step 1: approve_claim pays only up to the claimed amount, so 1,800 on a claim of 1,800 passes. Step 2: the same rule refuses 5,000 with a structured error that the model can read. Step 3: purge_claim refuses any caller without the admin role, so a delete needs a server-side role, not only a polite prompt. Step 4: in step 2 of the lab, tool_filter hides purge_claim from our model, but MCP clients other than ADK can still connect to this server, so the check must live here. Think of a bank vault: the teller's screen hides the vault button, and the vault door still has its own lock. A likely question: "Why not just remove purge_claim from the server?" Other clients, such as an admin console, may need it; each client filters what its own model may see, and the server enforces the role.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 1 of 4 · stdout

One print() on stdout breaks the JSON-RPC stream

claims_agent/claims_server.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("server ready")         # stdout
    mcp.run()
claims_agent/claims_server.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.info("server ready")  # stderr
    mcp.run()
This is the most common stdio bug. Over stdio, stdout is not a console: it is the wire that carries JSON-RPC messages between McpToolset and the server. Step 1 shows a harmless-looking print("server ready") at startup. Step 2: that line enters the stream, the client cannot parse it as JSON-RPC, and the session dies; adk web logs "ConnectionError: Failed to create MCP session". Step 3: the fix is logging.info, because the server set up logging on stderr, and stderr goes to the terminal, not to the client. Step 4: the stream is clean again and the log line still reaches you. Think of stdout as a fax line: if you say one word into it, the fax fails. A likely question: "Does a print inside a tool break it too?" Yes, any write to stdout at any time corrupts the stream, so search the server and its libraries for print calls.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 2 of 4 · filter

tool_filter and a prefix decide which tools the model sees

adk web .prompt: "What is the status of CLM-1002?"
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent.py · excerpt
import pathlib, sys
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import McpToolset, StdioConnectionParams
from mcp import StdioServerParameters
SERVER = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "claims_server.py"
claims_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StdioConnectionParams(
        server_params=StdioServerParameters(
            command=sys.executable, args=[str(SERVER)]),  # same venv
        timeout=10.0),                          # default 5.0 s
    tool_filter=["get_claim", "approve_claim"],  # no purge_claim
    tool_name_prefix="claims",                  # claims_get_claim
)
# root_agent = LlmAgent(..., tools=[claims_tools]): next slide

This is step 2 of the Acme claims desk: the agent connects to the claims MCP server from step 1 and gets only the tools it needs. Step 1: use StdioConnectionParams so you can set the timeout to 10 seconds; its default is 5.0 seconds, and a bare StdioServerParameters has no timeout at all. sys.executable starts the server in the agent's own virtual environment, so mcp is importable; a bare "python" on Windows often finds a different interpreter. Step 2: tool_filter matches the server's original names, so purge_claim stops at the bar and never reaches the model. Step 3: tool_name_prefix renames the rest, and the model calls claims_get_claim and claims_approve_claim; two servers can no longer collide on a name. Step 4: the model's list holds 2 of the 3 server tools. Think of a hotel key card: it opens two doors, and each door has a name plate. A likely question: "Does the filter use the prefixed name?" No, the filter runs first on the server's names, and ADK adds the prefix afterwards.

A payout rule pauses calls over $1,000 for a human

def payout_needs_human(**kwargs) -> bool:  # gets the call's args
    return float(kwargs.get("approved_amount", 0)) > 1000

claims_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=...,              # as on the last slide
    tool_filter=["get_claim", "approve_claim"],
    require_confirmation=payout_needs_human,
    tool_name_prefix="claims",
)
root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="claims_desk",
    model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    instruction=("You help claims adjusters. Look up a claim before "
                 "approving it. Pay at most the claimed amount."),
    tools=[claims_tools],

Three layers: filter hides, confirm gates, server checks.

Still step 2: some calls are allowed, but only with a human yes. Step 1: payout_needs_human is a plain function. ADK calls it with the arguments of the call, and with **kwargs one rule covers every tool of the toolset; 1,800 dollars is over the limit, so it returns True. Step 2: require_confirmation on the toolset attaches the rule to every tool it exposes. Step 3: run it. The model looks up the claim first, as the instruction says, then ADK emits adk_request_confirmation before approve_claim runs, and adk web shows a Confirm dialog. On Confirm the tool runs; on Reject the model gets "This tool call is rejected." Step 4: the rule sees the arguments the model sent, so if the model sends 999, no human is asked. That is why the server keeps its own limit. Least privilege has three layers: the filter hides, the confirmation gates, and the server checks. Think of a bank teller: big withdrawals need a manager's signature, and the vault still has its own lock. A likely question: "Where does the approval go in production?" The reply is a function response with the same id as the adk_request_confirmation call, so a Slack bot or a web form can send it.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 3 of 4 · HTTP server

The claims handbook runs as a streamable HTTP MCP server

python claims_agent/handbook_server.py
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/handbook_server.py · excerpt
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer
mcp = MCPServer("claims-handbook-server")
POLICIES = {
    "glass": "Glass repair: no deductible on comprehensive policies.",
    "rental": "Rental car covered up to 30 days at $40 per day.",
    "towing": "Towing covered up to 50 miles per incident.",
}
@mcp.tool()
def search_policy(topic: str) -> str:
    """Search the claims handbook. topic: glass, rental or towing."""
    return POLICIES.get(topic.lower(), f"No policy for '{topic}'.")
# list_topics(): same pattern, returns sorted(POLICIES)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # mcp 2.x: host and port go to run(); the path defaults to /mcp
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="127.0.0.1", port=3000)

It keeps running when an agent stops.

This is step 3 of the Acme claims desk: the claims handbook runs as its own MCP server over streamable HTTP, in terminal 2. Step 1: the tool looks the same as on stdio; the decorator, the docstring and the type hints define it. Step 2: the difference is the transport. In mcp 2.x, host and port go to run(), not to the MCPServer constructor, and the endpoint path defaults to /mcp, so the agent URL must end in /mcp. Step 3: a stdio server is a child process of one agent and dies with it; an HTTP server is a network service that many agents share, here the claims desk, a triage agent and an audit agent, and it keeps running when an agent stops. Think of the stdio server as a cook inside one restaurant, and the HTTP server as a supplier across the street that many restaurants use. A likely question: "When do I choose HTTP?" When several agents or teams share the tools, when the server needs its own scaling or deploy cycle, or when it runs in another language or host.

Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 4 of 4 · tenants

header_provider sends each broker's identity, not the prompt

adk api_server --with_ui .broker = an agency that uses the desk (a tenant)
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent.py · excerpt
from google.adk.agents.readonly_context import ReadonlyContext
def tenant_headers(ctx: ReadonlyContext) -> dict[str, str]:
    # user: state is set at login, never by the model
    tenant = ctx.state.get("user:tenant")
    if not tenant:
        raise ValueError("no user:tenant in state")  # fail closed
    return {"X-Tenant-ID": tenant}
handbook_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(...),  # step 3
    tool_filter=["search_policy", "list_topics"],
    tool_name_prefix="handbook",
    header_provider=tenant_headers,  # one session per identity
)

A prompt injection cannot change a header.

This is step 4 of the Acme claims desk: several brokers share the handbook server, so each request must carry the broker's identity. A broker here is an insurance agency that uses the desk, one tenant. Step 1: tenant_headers reads user:tenant from session state. State with the user: prefix belongs to one user and lasts across that user's sessions; your login code sets it, never the model. If it is missing, raise, so a request never falls back to another tenant's data: the middle pill shows that fail-closed path. Step 2: header_provider sends the value as the X-Tenant-ID header, and ADK pools one MCP session per header identity, so two brokers never share a session. Step 3: identity travels in headers, outside the conversation, so text in a prompt or a tool result cannot switch the tenant. Think of a hotel key card: identity travels with the card, not with what the guest says at the desk. A likely question: "Can header_provider be async?" Yes, it gets a ReadonlyContext per session and may be async, for example to look up a token.

The header comes from session state, so something must put the tenant there before the first message. Step 1: your login step creates the session with user:tenant already set. adk api_server --with_ui serves the ADK REST API next to the dev UI, so here we use curl against /apps/claims_agent/users/broker-b/sessions; in production your web app does the same call after it checks the user. Step 2: the response shows the session and its state; open that session in the UI. Step 3: from now on every handbook call carries X-Tenant-ID: broker-b, read by tenant_headers. The model never writes this value: it comes from login, through state, into a header. Think of the front desk that codes your hotel key card before you reach the lift. A likely question: "What happens in adk web without this step?" tenant_headers raises, the handbook toolset fails closed, and the agent answers without handbook tools; the gotcha slides show how to alert on that.
Lab 6 Acme claims desk · step 4 of 4 · tool cache

tools/list is cached per identity for 300 s, then filtered again

labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent.py · excerpt
handbook_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(...),  # step 3
    tool_filter=["search_policy", "list_topics"],  # review new tools
    header_provider=tenant_headers,
    tool_list_cache_ttl_seconds=300,   # tools/list reused for 5 minutes
)
# ADK does not subscribe to notifications/tools/list_changed
# ttl=0 raises ValueError; ttl=None turns the cache off

new_tool is listed after the TTL, and tool_filter still hides it.

handbook :3000/mcp
search_policy
list_topics
new_tool
cache · broker-alisted 2 · shown 2
cache · broker-blisted 2 · shown 2
One more detail of the HTTP toolset: ADK caches the tools/list answer. Step 1: tool_list_cache_ttl_seconds=300 keeps each list for five minutes, and the cache is keyed like the session pool, so each header identity, here each broker, has its own entry and its own clock. Step 2: the server team deploys a new tool. ADK does not subscribe to the tools/list_changed notification, so both caches still say "listed 2" until their entries expire. Step 3: when each clock runs out, the next call lists 3 tools, but the agent still shows 2, because tool_filter lists only the two tools we reviewed. Step 4: that is the point of the filter: a server-side change cannot widen the agent's action space without a code review. A value of 0 raises ValueError; use None to turn the cache off. Think of a restaurant menu that is reprinted every five minutes, but the waiter only offers the dishes the manager approved. A likely question: "Why did my new server tool not appear?" The cache had not expired yet, or tool_filter does not list it.
Build · Acme claims desk · REST API

OpenAPIToolset reads the spec, and the key comes from the env

CLAIMS_API_KEY=demo-key-123 uvicorn claims_api:app --port 8081terminal 1
claim_tool.py · hand-written
def get_claim_status(claim_id: str) -> dict:
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:8081/claims/{claim_id}"
    key = {"X-API-Key": "demo-key-123"}  # in git
    return httpx.get(url, headers=key).json()
claim_tool = FunctionTool(get_claim_status)

One tool from the spec. The key never enters git.

labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent.py · excerpt
# imports: OpenAPIToolset, token_to_scheme_credential
SPEC_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8081/openapi.json"
spec = httpx.get(SPEC_URL, timeout=5).json()   # at import time
auth_scheme, auth_credential = token_to_scheme_credential(
    "apikey", "header", "X-API-Key", os.environ["CLAIMS_API_KEY"])
claims_status = OpenAPIToolset(
    spec_dict=spec,
    auth_scheme=auth_scheme,
    auth_credential=auth_credential,
    tool_filter=["get_claim_status"],   # snake_case(operationId)
    allow_private_network_access=True,  # 127.0.0.1: dev only
)
# root_agent: tools=[claims_tools, handbook_tools, claims_status]
Now claims_desk gets its third tool source, the claims-status REST service from terminal 1. Step 1 shows the version to avoid: a hand-written httpx tool with the URL and the API key in the source, so the key ends up in git. The service already publishes an OpenAPI spec, so let ADK build the tool. Step 2: OpenAPIToolset reads the spec, and token_to_scheme_credential turns the key from the CLAIMS_API_KEY environment variable into the X-API-Key header. os.environ with square brackets fails at startup when the key is missing, instead of falling back to a value in the code. Step 3: tool_filter uses the generated tool name, which the next slide explains. Step 4: allow_private_network_access=True is needed only because the API runs on 127.0.0.1; the gotcha after next shows the guard it lifts. agent.py downloads the spec when it is imported, so start claims_api before adk web. Think of the spec as a menu with item numbers: the agent orders by the number, not by describing the dish. A likely question: "Where should the key live in production?" In Secret Manager or the deploy environment, never in the instruction or the code.
Build · Acme claims desk · REST API

ADK names each REST tool after its operationId, in snake_case

labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_api.py · excerpt
app = FastAPI(title="Claims Status API",
              servers=[{"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8081"}])
api_key = APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key")
@app.get("/claims/{claim_id}", operation_id="getClaimStatus",
         dependencies=[Depends(check_key)])
def get_claim_status(claim_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get the review stage, adjuster and next step for a claim."""
    if claim_id not in STATUS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="unknown claim")
    return STATUS[claim_id]
output · illustrative
user: Status of CLM-1001?
desk: get_claim_status {"claim_id": "CLM-1001"}
desk: R. Patel is assigned. Next step 2026-10-26.
How does the spec become a tool? Step 1: set operation_id in FastAPI, here getClaimStatus. Without it, FastAPI generates a long id from the function and path, and the tool name changes whenever the route changes. Step 2: ADK's operation parser makes one tool per operation and names it snake_case of the operationId, cut to 60 characters, so getClaimStatus becomes get_claim_status. tool_filter must use that generated name, not the operationId; if you are not sure, print [t.name for t in await claims_status.get_tools()]. Step 3: the servers entry in the spec gives the base URL, and the model calls get_claim_status with the claim id. With a wrong key, the tool returns the 401 as an execution error that the model can read. Think of the operationId as the item number on a menu: keep it stable, and the order always reaches the right dish. A likely question: "What if my API needs camelCase parameters?" Pass preserve_property_names=True; otherwise ADK converts them to snake_case.
Gotcha OpenAPIToolset

The SSRF guard blocks 127.0.0.1 until you allow private access

SymptomThe tool result says Tool get_claim_status execution failed. ... Execution Error: Blocked host: 127.0.0.1 Causeallow_private_network_access=False by default. Loopback, private, link-local (cloud metadata), *.internal and *.local are refused. FixSet it to True for a dev or internal API only. In production, call a public or VPC-routed hostname.
This is the error you hit the first time OpenAPIToolset calls a local API. Step 1: the tool does not raise; it returns an error result that ends in "Execution Error: Blocked host: 127.0.0.1". Step 2: the cause is ADK's SSRF guard. By default, REST API tools refuse loopback, private and link-local addresses, which include the cloud metadata service, plus names such as localhost, metadata.goog and anything under .internal or .local. Public hostnames pass. Step 3: allow_private_network_access=True lets 127.0.0.1 through, which is right for this lab, but it lifts the guard for every private host, including the metadata endpoint, which holds cloud credentials. So keep it for a dev or internal API only, and in production call a public or VPC-routed hostname. Note that MCP connections do not go through this check. Think of a mail room that refuses letters addressed to the vault: turning that rule off for your desk turns it off for the vault too. A likely question: "Why is metadata dangerous?" A prompt-injected URL could make the agent fetch the instance's service-account token; the paper slides show SSRF to metadata in real MCP servers.
Build · Acme claims desk · errors

Write tool errors as the next tool call, not a terminal command

claims_agent/claims_server.py · get_claim · developer-style
    if not SESSION["valid"]:
        return {"status": "error", "message": "Session expired. "
                "Run `claims-cli login` and retry."}
claims_agent/claims_server.py · adds login · agent-style
@mcp.tool()
def login() -> dict:
    """Start a claims session. Call it when a session expired."""
    SESSION["valid"] = True
    return {"status": "ok"}
# in get_claim; also add "login" to tool_filter
    if not SESSION["valid"]:
        return {"status": "error", "message": "Session expired. Call "
                "claims_login, then call claims_get_claim again."}
arXiv 2609.35381 · MCP error messages written for developers
An error message is a prompt: the model reads it and tries to do what it says. arXiv 2609.35381 (2026-09-28) audited 3,001 errors from 150 popular MCP servers; 949 of them prescribe a next step, and 62 of 67 credential steps ask for a terminal command, a config change or a web page, which a tool-only agent cannot do. Step 1 shows that style on our own server: "Run claims-cli login". With a terminal step, mean recovery from an expired credential was 45%. Step 2: add a login tool and name it the way the model sees it: with tool_name_prefix="claims" that is claims_login, and login must also go into tool_filter. Naming a login tool lifted recovery to 84%. Step 3: for rate limits, "Wait before retrying." gave 6% recovery, and naming the call to repeat gave 88%. The study used five OpenAI models on BFCL-style tasks, so treat the numbers as direction, not as a guarantee for Gemini. Think of a note on a locked door: "Ask reception for a key" helps a person, but a robot needs "press button 2". A likely question: "Why not just retry in code?" Do both: back off in code for 429s, and still tell the model which call to repeat.
Build · Acme claims desk · errors

For servers you cannot edit, a plugin drops the human-only step

labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent_errors.py
import re
from google.adk.plugins.base_plugin import BasePlugin
HUMAN_STEP = re.compile(r"\b(Run|Open|Edit) [^.]*\.\s*")  # human-only
class AgentErrorPlugin(BasePlugin):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(name="agent_errors")
    async def after_tool_callback(
            self, *, tool, tool_args, tool_context, result):
        text = str(result)
        if "error" not in text.lower():
            return None                     # normal results pass
        cleaned = HUMAN_STEP.sub("", text)  # keep the cause
        return {"result": cleaned} if cleaned != text else None
# register once: App(..., plugins=[AgentErrorPlugin()])
Our own server now writes agent-style errors, but third-party MCP servers will not. A plugin fixes their text in one place for every tool. Step 1: a regular expression finds human-only steps, sentences that start with Run, Open or Edit. Step 2: after_tool_callback runs after every tool call; normal results pass through untouched, so the plugin only touches errors. Step 3: it deletes the human-only sentence and keeps the cause; a non-None return replaces the result the model reads. The same paper measured cause-only errors at 82% recovery, against 45% with the terminal step. Step 4: register the plugin once on the App, and it covers every agent and tool in the app; the lab keeps that App block as an option at the end of agent.py. Think of an interpreter who leaves out the parts of a message that only apply to someone else. A likely question: "Why a regex and not a model call?" A regex is deterministic and free; the paper also tested a one-sentence prompt that deletes the step, with the same 82%, if your errors are too varied for a pattern.
Gotcha MCP install

Two loud MCP failures: a missing extra and a renamed SDK

1 · the import fails SymptomImportError: cannot import name 'McpToolset' from 'google.adk.tools.mcp_tool' Causemcp is not installed. ADK logs the real error only at debug level. Fixpip install "google-adk[mcp]==2.13.0"
2 · v1 server code on mcp 2.3.0 SymptomNo module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'. This is mcp 2.x, where FastMCP was renamed to MCPServer ... CauseFastMCP is now MCPServer. host and port moved to run(). FixThe diff below, or pin mcp<2.
claims_agent/handbook_server.py · mcp 1.x → 2.x
# mcp 1.x: fails on mcp 2.3.0
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
mcp = FastMCP("claims-handbook-server", port=3000)
# mcp 2.x: the name changed, and host and port go to run()
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer
mcp = MCPServer("claims-handbook-server")
mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="127.0.0.1", port=3000)
Docs MCP SDK v2 migration
These two failures are loud, but their messages point the wrong way. Step 1: in google-adk 2.13.0, mcp is an optional extra. Without it, importing McpToolset fails with an ImportError that names McpToolset, because tools/mcp_tool/__init__.py catches the real ImportError and logs it only at debug level. Install google-adk with the mcp extra. Step 2: old tutorials use FastMCP. The mcp 2.x SDK renamed it to MCPServer, and mcp 2.3.0 raises a ModuleNotFoundError whose text tells you so; if you pass port to the constructor, you get a TypeError about an unexpected keyword argument. Step 3: the fix is a three-line diff. Step 4: in 2.x, the constructor takes only the name, and host and port go to run(). If you cannot migrate yet, pin mcp below 2. Think of a shop that moved to a new address: the old sign says "closed", but the shop is open around the corner. A likely question: "Does ADK need mcp 2.x?" No, ADK accepts mcp from 1.24 up to 3, so the server code decides the version you pin.
Gotcha MCP at runtime

When a toolset fails to load, the agent keeps talking without it

SymptomNo exception. The agent answers without its tools. CauseServer crash, a print() on stdout, a URL without /mcp, or a start slower than timeout. FixAlert on the log line. Run a smoke test at startup.

Before 2.10 / 2.11, a dead session came back as a normal result: Session terminated. Alert on that string too.

The third MCP failure is the expensive one, because nothing turns red. Step 1: the claims server exits, the toolset cannot load, and ADK logs one line: "Agent claims_desk will run without the tools from toolset McpToolset (prefix 'claims'), which failed to load". The agent keeps running and tells the adjuster "I can't access claims". Step 2: the usual causes are a server crash, a print on stdout, a URL without /mcp, or a server that starts slower than the timeout. Step 3: you own the alert: match that log line in your logging system, and run a startup smoke test, which is the next slide. Step 4: in versions before 2.10 and 2.11, after a server restart or a scale-to-zero, ADK kept the dead session and returned "MCP tool execution failed: Session terminated" as a normal tool result, so alert on that error string too, not only on exceptions. Think of a phone line that goes dead while the operator keeps talking politely to the caller. A likely question: "Why does ADK not just raise?" One broken toolset should not take down an agent that has other working tools, so the choice is deliberate.
Gotcha MCP at runtime · the fix

A startup smoke test fails loudly when a toolset does not load

python smoke_test.py
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/smoke_test.py
import asyncio
from claims_agent.agent import claims_tools
EXPECTED = {"get_claim", "approve_claim", "login"}
async def main() -> None:
    try:
        tools = await claims_tools.get_tools()
    except Exception as exc:  # crash, print, bad path, timeout
        raise SystemExit(f"FAIL toolset did not load: {exc!r}")
    names = {t.name.removeprefix("claims_") for t in tools}
    if names != EXPECTED:
        raise SystemExit(f"FAIL expected {EXPECTED}, got {names}")
    print("OK", sorted(names))
asyncio.run(main())
output · illustrative · two runs
$ python smoke_test.py  # print() in server
FAIL toolset did not load: ConnectionError(...)
$ python smoke_test.py  # fixed
OK ['approve_claim', 'get_claim', 'login']

Run it in CI and before each deploy. A non-zero exit stops the rollout.

Docs adk.dev MCP tools
The fix for the silent failure is to make it loud before traffic arrives. Step 1: the smoke test imports the same claims_tools object the agent uses and calls get_tools(), which starts the stdio server and lists its tools; any crash, stdout print, wrong path or timeout raises here, and SystemExit turns it into a non-zero exit code. Step 2: it also compares the names with the expected set, so a server that drops a tool, or a tool_filter typo, fails too. The prefix is removed before the compare. Step 3: the output shows two runs: the first with a print in the server, the second after the fix. Step 4: run it in CI and as a deploy gate. The full file is in the lab folder; it needs claims_api running, because agent.py fetches the OpenAPI spec when it is imported. Think of a pilot's pre-flight checklist: the plane can fly without it, until the day it cannot. A likely question: "Why remove the prefix before the compare?" get_tools returns the names the model sees, with the claims_ prefix, while EXPECTED uses the server's names, the same names as tool_filter.
arXiv Jul 2026

Most public MCP servers have no OAuth, and many vanish in days

arXiv 2608.00150 2026-07-31

Exposed by Design: A Dynamic Security Assessment of Internet-Facing MCP Servers at Scale

A live audit of 414 internet-facing MCP servers. 91.8% lack OAuth. 68 vulnerabilities, including SSRF to cloud metadata.
Connect only to remote servers with OAuth. Keep metadata hosts blocked in production.
Paper arXiv 2608.00150
Three papers from the last three months change how the Acme desk picks and runs MCP servers; this is the first. Step 1: the authors found 414 MCP servers on the public internet and tested them live, not from their code. Step 2: 91.8% of them have no OAuth, so anyone who finds the URL can call their tools. Step 3: they found 68 vulnerabilities, including SSRF to cloud metadata, the same class of attack that the OpenAPI guard blocks, and 41.6% of the servers were gone within three days, so a public server is also unstable. Step 4: what to change on Monday: connect only to remote servers that use OAuth, pin and review what you connect to, and keep metadata hosts blocked in production. Think of a public MCP server like a stranger's USB stick: useful, maybe, but you check it before you plug it in. A likely question: "Does ADK support OAuth for MCP?" Yes, McpToolset takes auth_scheme and auth_credential, and ADK asks for the credential with adk_request_credential before it lists tools.
arXiv Oct 2026

Approving one MCP call is not a sandbox for the server process

arXiv 2610.22301 2026-10-15

My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale

787 of 4,806 triaged servers (16.4%) touch the filesystem despite non-filesystem labels. 150 confirmed vulnerable.
Run stdio servers in a container with one mounted directory. Check path arguments in before_tool_callback.
Paper arXiv 2610.22301
The second paper shows why a human "yes" is not enough. Step 1: the authors triaged 4,806 MCP servers; 787 of them, 16.4%, touch the filesystem even though their labels say something else, and 150 were confirmed vulnerable, with 13 advisories and 2 CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP server. Step 2: a tool called get_weather can open your cloud credentials file, because approving one call trusts the whole server process, with your user's file permissions. Step 3: the real boundary is the process: run stdio servers in a container that mounts one directory, here the claims documents. Step 4: also check path arguments against an allow-list in before_tool_callback, so a tool cannot even ask for a file outside it. Think of approval like letting a plumber into the house: you approved the sink, but he can walk into every room unless you lock the doors. A likely question: "Is tool_filter enough?" It limits what the model can call, but not what the server process can do, so you need the container too.
arXiv Oct 2026

The parameter schema, not the name, decides which tool is picked

arXiv 2610.14334 2026-10-09

Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP?

Flat params were chosen 93.3-100% on Create Issue. Renaming to to recipient_id cut selection to 1-10%. With names-only differences, the first-listed tool won 92-100%.
Use flat, well-named params. Dedupe near-duplicate tools with tool_filter. Shuffle tool order in evals.
Paper arXiv 2610.14334
The third paper asks what makes a model pick one MCP tool over another when two look alike. Step 1: it varied one metadata factor at a time. Flat, top-level parameters were chosen 93.3 to 100% of the time on a Create Issue task. Step 2: the parameter schema is the strongest lever: renaming the parameter "to" to "recipient_id" cut the selection of an otherwise equal tool to 1 to 10%. Step 3: when only the names differ, list order decides: the first-listed tool won 92 to 100% of the time. Step 4: what to change on Monday: design flat, well-named parameters, remove near-duplicate tools with tool_filter, and shuffle tool order in your evals so order does not hide a bad schema. Think of two identical doors: people take the one with the clearer handle, and if the handles match, the one nearest to them. A likely question: "Does the docstring not matter?" It does, but in this study the schema moved selection more than the description.
In production Uber · Aug 2026

Uber: MCP tool schemas cost 50K-70K tokens on every request

50K-70K tokens of MCP tool schemas per request, "for 100+ tools".
Uber's fix: resolve tools through a CLI gateway, or search tools on demand.

Acme: set tool_filter on every toolset and count schema tokens per request.

Post Uber: Running a Software Factory Efficiently
Uber published its cost program for agentic coding on 2026-08-27. One line item is the MCP tool schema: about 50K to 70K tokens for 100+ tools, paid on every request before the model reads a word of the task. Step 1: the schemas pile up on each request. Step 2: their fixes are a gateway that resolves tools through a CLI, and on-demand tool search, so the model sees only the tools the task needs. Step 3: for Acme, the cheap version of the same idea is tool_filter on every toolset, and a metric for schema tokens per request, so a new server cannot quietly double your bill. Think of a mechanic who carries the whole workshop to every job instead of the two tools the job needs. L'Oreal also connects ADK agents to its data through MCP, but published no cost number. A likely question: "Is there a tool count limit?" No hard limit, so measure tokens and selection accuracy as you add tools; the next slide shows what code mode and grouping add.
In production Uber · MCPacific

Code mode cut one wide-table query from 1,431,594 to 900 tokens

arXiv 2610.05319 MCPacific · 2026-10-04
1.33M MCP tool specs map to 58,915 capabilities. A capability hierarchy beats a flat list by up to +12 pp in crowded sets.
Group tools by server before the model picks one.
Acme: past about 50 tools, give each MCP server its own AgentTool subagent.
Post Uber arXiv 2610.05319
Code mode goes one step further than tool search: the model writes a short script that batches tool calls, so intermediate results never pass through the context. Step 1: in Uber's post, one wide-table query fell from 1,431,594 tokens to 900; the bars use a log scale, because the drop is more than three orders of magnitude. Step 2: a small case gains much less: one SQL example went from 903 to 402 tokens. Uber has 25+ pre-built code-mode skills. The same post reports grounding through a context graph with 24M nodes: a grounded query took 38 seconds and was correct, the ungrounded one took 20 minutes and was wrong. Step 3: the MCPacific paper mapped 1.33 million MCP tool specs to 58,915 capabilities and found that a capability hierarchy beats a flat list by up to 12 points when many tools compete. Step 4: for Acme, past about 50 tools, give each MCP server its own AgentTool subagent, which is a two-level hierarchy. The 50 is a rule of thumb, not a limit, so measure. Think of a large shop: you find a screwdriver faster through the aisle signs than by reading every shelf. A likely question: "Does ADK have code mode?" ADK has code executors; the slide shows Uber's numbers, not an ADK feature.
Best practices · tool surface and identity

Least privilege for MCP tools: five checks for every toolset

  • tool_filter on every toolset. New server tools need a review.
  • tool_name_prefix per server. Merged namespaces raise tool hallucination.
  • require_confirmation on money, delete and send. The server checks too.
  • Identity in headers via header_provider. Never in the prompt.
  • A default tenant when user:tenant is missing. Fail closed.
labs/adk/lab6-acme-claims-desk/claims_agent/agent.py · excerpt
claims_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StdioConnectionParams(...),  # step 2
    tool_filter=["get_claim", "approve_claim", "login"],
    tool_name_prefix="claims",
    require_confirmation=payout_needs_human,
)
handbook_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(...),  # step 3
    tool_filter=["search_policy", "list_topics"],
    tool_name_prefix="handbook",
    header_provider=tenant_headers,  # raises without a tenant
    tool_list_cache_ttl_seconds=300,
)
This slide and the next are the review list for every toolset the Acme claims desk mounts. Each check maps to one line of the final agent.py on the right. Check 1: tool_filter on every toolset, so a tool the server team adds needs a code review before the model can call it. Check 2: one prefix per server, because merged namespaces are where tool hallucination is worst (arXiv 2609.19425 collected 322 real cases across 10 models). Check 3: require_confirmation on money, delete and send tools, while the server keeps its own authorisation, because other MCP clients can call it. Check 4: identity travels in headers from header_provider, never in the prompt. Check 5, a don't: never fall back to a default tenant when user:tenant is missing; raise instead, so one broker never sees another broker's data. Think of a building pass: the badge lists the doors you may open, and each door still has its own lock. A likely question: "Is the prefix only cosmetic?" No, it also stops two servers that both expose search from colliding on one name.
Best practices · isolation and operations

Contain the server process, and make every failure loud

  • stdio servers in a container with one mount. 16.4% launder file access.
  • allow_private_network_access=True in production.
  • Pin google-adk, mcp and server versions.
  • Errors say "<cause>. Call <tool>". Recovery 45% → 84%.
  • Smoke-test get_tools(). Alert on "will run without the tools".
  • print() in a stdio server. stdout carries JSON-RPC.
The second half of the review list is about the process around the tools. Check 1: run stdio servers in a container with one mounted directory, because 16.4% of triaged servers reach the filesystem beyond their label, and never set allow_private_network_access=True in production, because it opens the metadata endpoint too. Check 2: pin google-adk, mcp and the server versions, since the 2.x SDK rename shows how a minor upgrade breaks server code. Check 3: write errors as "cause, then the tool to call", which lifted recovery from 45% to 84% in arXiv 2609.35381. Check 4: smoke-test get_tools() at startup and alert on the "will run without the tools" log line, and never print to stdout in a stdio server. The picture shows the layers from the outside in: the container, the server's own checks, the confirmation gate, and the filter with its prefix, around the model; the alerts watch all of them. Think of an onion: an attacker who gets through one layer still meets the next. A likely question: "Which layer would you add first?" tool_filter, because it is one line and it shrinks everything after it.
07

A2A, Skills and Plugins

Build the Acme refund team: one refund agent, served over MCP and A2A, with a refund Skill and one app-wide cap.

1 · MCP toolAny MCP host calls the agent.
2 · A2A serviceAnother team's agent delegates to it.
3 · SkillInstructions the model loads on demand.
4 · PluginOne hook for every agent in the App.
This chapter takes one refund agent and makes it reusable in four ways, and the hero animation shows all four. First we expose it as a single MCP tool, so any MCP host can call it; then we expose the same agent over A2A with an agent card on port 8001, and a support triage agent owned by another team delegates refund tickets to it. Next the refund policy moves into an Agent Skill that the model loads only when a refund question arrives, and finally one plugin enforces the $500 cap on every agent in the App. Note the dashed links: refund_agent does not call the MCP tool or the card, it is exposed as them. Rule of thumb: with MCP the caller sees one tool and you own the contract; with A2A the caller sees an agent and the other team owns its prompt, state and lifecycle. Think of MCP as a power socket with a fixed shape, and A2A as calling another department. Pins for the whole chapter: Python 3.11+, google-adk 2.13.0 with the mcp and a2a extras, mcp 2.3.0, a2a-sdk 1.2.3; every file is in labs/adk/lab7-acme-refunds. A likely question: "Why not always use A2A?" Because the A2A boundary also cuts session state and adds a trust boundary, which the gotcha and paper slides cover.

Codelab Getting Started with MCP, ADK and A2A
Before step 1, set up one folder that the whole lab grows in: labs/adk/lab7-acme-refunds, with a README that has the same commands. Install the pinned versions with the mcp and a2a extras, and export the Gemini variables in every terminal, because plain python and uvicorn do not read an agent folder's .env file the way adk web does. The ADK_SUPPRESS_EXPERIMENTAL_FEATURE_WARNINGS variable silences the warning from to_mcp_server, which is experimental. Walk the three terminals: terminal 1 runs the MCP server only for step 1; terminal 3 runs the MCP consumer with adk run in step 1; terminal 2 runs the A2A server on 8001 for steps 2 and 3; terminal 3 then runs adk web on 8000 for steps 3 to 5. Each agent package for adk web needs an __init__.py with "from . import agent"; refund_service needs only an empty one. Think of the folder as one kitchen with three serving hatches. A likely question: "Which processes must run together?" Only in step 3: uvicorn on 8001 and adk web on 8000.
