conversation_plan holds the hidden fact and the goal.

The agent breaks its instruction and approves $820. Step 14 scores this.

The simulator sends </finished> when its goal is met.

EXPERT gives everything at once and pushes for a guarantee.

Step twelve: instead of a frozen conversation, an LLM plays the customer. A fixed golden script breaks as soon as the agent asks a clarifying question; a simulator answers it. The NOVICE persona knows its order is A-2040 but says so only when the agent asks. Think of a mystery shopper with a hidden brief: the conversation_plan holds the secret facts and the goal, and the simulator sends the finished tag when the goal is met. In this run the agent opened the ticket but also told the customer the 820 dollar refund was approved; models do not follow an instruction every time, and this is the slip the rubric must catch in step 14. The built-in personas are EXPERT, NOVICE and EVALUATOR. A likely question: "Are simulators realistic?" Not fully: research shows they over-cooperate and rarely give up like real users, so add a frustrated persona when you can.

Step thirteen: turn the scenarios into eval cases. adk eval_set create makes an empty set called refund_sim, stored as refund_agent/refund_sim.evalset.json, and add_eval_case reads scenarios.json plus session_input.json and adds one case per scenario. The case id is the first 8 hex characters of a SHA-256 of the scenario, and duplicates are skipped, so if you edit a scenario's text you get a new case and the old one stays in the set: delete it, or recreate the set. The message format comes from cli_tools_click.py; the ids shown are illustrative. Analogy: a library that files each book by a fingerprint of its text; change one word and it is a new book on the shelf. A likely question: "Can ADK write the scenarios for me?" Yes, adk eval_set generate_eval_cases can, but it needs the Agent Platform API and application default credentials.

Step fourteen scores the simulated chats. Simulated cases have no golden turns, so we use only reference-free metrics. sim_config.json has three of them: hallucinations_v1 checks that the answers are grounded in the tool results, per_turn_user_simulator_quality_v1 checks that the simulator followed its plan, and the rubric metric on this slide checks our two rules. A rubric is a property the answer must have; the judge scores each rubric five times. The type field picks the simulator; older configs without it are treated as llm_backed with a warning, and we cap the chat at 8 turns instead of the default 20. In the NOVICE chat the agent gave the ticket but promised the 820 dollar refund, so no_overlimit_promise scores 0.0, the rubric metric scores 0.5 and the case fails. The output is illustrative. A likely question: "Do these need Google Cloud?" No: these three metrics run on the AI Studio key; only safety_v1 and the multi_turn metrics need a Cloud project.

Step fifteen closes the loop like any bug fix: add one sentence to the instruction, "Never say that a refund above 500 USD is approved", run the same refund_sim set again, and keep it green. The output is illustrative; a real rerun can still flip on a close call, which is why the practices slide asks for at least three runs. Do not add tool_trajectory_avg_score or another reference-based metric to the simulated set: simulated cases have no golden turns, and the run fails with "expected_invocations is needed by this metric." Analogy: a regression test; the bug you fixed today stays fixed because the same test runs on every build. A likely question: "Is the rubric score enough to trust?" No: the paper slides show judges call failed chats satisfied, so we add a judge-free completion bit next.
Build · Lab 9 add-on · google-adk 2.13.0

Agents catch loud tool errors, but miss quiet wrong values

trace · A-1001 · lookup_order returns a plausible wrong value
lookup_order(order_id="A-1001")
# -> {"status": "success", "order_id": "A-1001", "amount": -79.0}
issue_refund(order_id="A-1001", amount=-79.0, reason="damaged")
# a negative refund charges the customer; refund_policy_score passes

A 503 is loud. A well-formed −79.0 is quiet.

Agents flag the loud fault 91.3% of the time, the quiet one 58.8%.

With nothing wrong, they still raise a false alarm 26.8% of the time.

arXiv 2610.10062
This add-on starts with a failure our eval gate cannot see. When a tool says HTTP 503, agents notice; when lookup_order returns a well-formed negative amount, they often do not. The paper arXiv 2610.10062 measured it: agents flag the loud fault 91.3 percent of the time, the quiet wrong value only 58.8 percent, and with nothing wrong they still raise a false alarm 26.8 percent of the time, so the quiet case is barely above guessing. Here the harm is real: a refund of minus 79 dollars charges the customer, and our 500 dollar metric still passes it, because minus 79 is below 500. The paper also found that a prompt line telling the model to check each result did not change detection, so the next slide puts the check in code. Analogy: a gas leak has no sound; you need a detector, not a sharper ear. A likely question: "Would the trajectory metric catch this?" No: the tools and their order are correct, only a value is wrong.
Build · Lab 9 add-on · google-adk 2.13.0

An after_tool_callback turns a wrong amount into an error

labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/refund_agent/agent.py · excerpt
class OutcomeContractPlugin(BasePlugin):
    RECOVERY = {"lookup_order": ["escalate_to_human"]}
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(name="outcome_contracts")
    async def after_tool_callback(self, *, tool, tool_args,
                                  tool_context, result):
        if tool.name != "lookup_order":
            return None                  # None: keep the tool result
        if result.get("status") != "success":
            return None
        amount = result.get("amount")
        if isinstance(amount, (int, float)) and amount > 0:
            return None
        return {"status": "error", "violated": "amount > 0",
                "recovery_tools": self.RECOVERY["lookup_order"]}

Return None: ADK keeps the tool result.

The contract: a looked-up amount must be above 0.

Return a dict: it replaces the result the model sees.

Name the next tool. Without it the gain disappears.

The fix is a check in code, not a line in the prompt. A plugin's after_tool_callback runs after every tool call with the tool, its args, the context and the result. Returning None keeps the result, so every other tool and every error passes through untouched. For lookup_order with status success, the contract is simple: the amount must be a number above 0. If it is not, the callback returns a dict, and that dict replaces the result the model sees: status error, the violated contract, and recovery_tools, the next tool to call. The Outcome Monitors paper, arXiv 2608.19303, shows the receipt must name a recovery tool: on the ToolMaze tool-use benchmark success went from 10.9 to 28.1 percent, and removing the tool list removed the gain. Analogy: a smoke detector wired into the pipe, with the exit sign lit. A likely question: "Why a plugin and not an agent callback?" A plugin on the App applies to every agent and tool in the app, so one contract covers the whole refund team.

from types import SimpleNamespace
from refund_agent.agent import OutcomeContractPlugin

def test_negative_amount_becomes_error():
    bad = {"status": "success", "order_id": "A-1001", "amount": -79.0}
    out = asyncio.run(OutcomeContractPlugin().after_tool_callback(
        tool=SimpleNamespace(name="lookup_order"), tool_args={},
        tool_context=None, result=bad))
    assert out["status"] == "error"
    assert out["recovery_tools"] == ["escalate_to_human"]

Wire the plugin into an App in agent.py: adk eval, adk web and adk api_server look for app before root_agent there, so the eval gate now runs with the contract on. Passing plugins to a Runner directly is deprecated in 2.x; the warning says to use the app argument. The lab file has a second test that a good amount, 79.0, returns None. The pytest output is illustrative. Analogy: you test a fuse with a test current, not by setting the house on fire. Gotcha Evals

A wrong config path or zero cases still gives a green run

Symptomrefund_policy_score is missing from the output. CauseA typo in the config path. ADK logs only Using default criteria. Fixtest -f the config first.
SymptomA green pipeline on a failing eval. CauseExit 0 before 2.13.0, and | tee hides the exit code. Fixpipefail, then count the cases that ran.
Issue #6951 zero cases passed
labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/ci/eval_gate.sh · excerpt
set -euo pipefail
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD
CFG=refund_agent/test_config.json
test -f "$CFG" || { echo "missing $CFG"; exit 1; }

adk eval refund_agent refund_agent/refund.evalset.json \
  --config_file_path="$CFG" --print_detailed_results | tee eval.log
N=$(grep -c '^Eval Id:' eval.log || true)
test "$N" -eq 2 || { echo "ran $N of 2 cases"; exit 1; }
grep -q 'Metric: refund_policy_score' eval.log || exit 1
Two failures that look like success: the pipeline is green, so nobody looks. First: a typo in the config path is not an error. ADK logs "No config file supplied or file not found. Using default criteria." and scores with the two defaults, so the 500 dollar rule never runs; the gate script checks that the file exists first. Second: before 2.13.0 adk eval always exited 0, and a pipe into tee hides the exit code unless pipefail is on, so the script sets pipefail and also counts the cases that ran; update that number when you add cases. On the pytest path, before 2.10.0 AgentEvaluator also passed an evalset with zero cases, issue 6951; 2.13.0 raises "No eval cases were evaluated". The last line checks that our own metric really ran. Analogy: test the smoke alarm with smoke, not by looking at the green light. A likely question: "Is the case count not brittle?" Yes, a little, and that is the point: adding a case should be a conscious change to the gate.
Gotcha Evals

safety_v1 flipped its scale, so keep a case that must fail

SymptomHarmful answers pass the safety_v1 gate. Causesafety_v1 resolved to safety_v3, which scores the other way. FixPin both packages. Keep a known-bad case that must fail.
labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/ci/eval_gate.sh · end
# known-bad: expects issue_refund on A-2040, so it MUST fail
if adk eval refund_agent refund_agent/known_bad.evalset.json \
     --config_file_path="$CFG"; then
  echo "gate passed a known-bad case"; exit 1
fi
Issue #7258 safety_v1 flip
A third silent failure: the metric itself changes meaning. safety_v1 resolved to the unversioned latest safety metric, which became safety_v3 and scores in the opposite direction, issue 7258; it is fixed in 2.10.0, but the behaviour also depends on the google-cloud-aiplatform version, so pin both. Watch the fixture table: with a sound metric, the known-good case passes and the known-bad case fails; after the flip both results invert, and only the known-bad fixture tells you. The gate script ends with exactly that: known_bad.evalset.json is a copy of the A-2040 case that expects issue_refund for 820 dollars, so a correct agent must fail it, and if adk eval exits 0 the gate stops. Analogy: you test a scale with a known weight before you trust it. A likely question: "Why does the known-bad case fail on a correct agent?" The correct agent escalates instead of refunding, so the trajectory metric does not match the expected issue_refund call.
arXiv Sep 2026

Of simulated chats judged satisfied, 57.5% had failed the task

arXiv 2609.12191 2026-09-10

GAUGE: when not to trust an LLM judge in user-simulated evals

25 agents, simulated customers. Of chats rated satisfied, 57.5% failed the task. On close agent pairs, judge and real reward disagree 31%.
Add a judge-free completion bit.
arXiv 2609.12191 GAUGE
GAUGE, from September 2026, ran 25 agents with simulated customers on tau-squared-bench and SimulatorArena, then compared the LLM judge's verdict with the real task outcome. Of the chats the judge rated satisfied, 57.5 percent had failed the customer's task. On close pairs, meaning two agents with similar scores, the judge and the real reward disagreed 31 percent of the time, against under 1 percent for clearly different agents. The scatter is schematic: 80 chats, 40 rated satisfied, and 23 of those 40, which is 57.5 percent, turn red because the task failed. The Monday change is a judge-free completion bit next to every rubric, which the next slides build. Analogy: a polite customer saying "thanks" is not the same as the parcel arriving. A likely question: "So should I drop the judge?" No: keep it for tone and meaning, but never let it alone decide whether the task was done.
arXiv Aug 2026

Six LLM judges plateau at 77-82% on hard tool-calling cases

arXiv 2608.26623 2026-08-27

AgentJudgeBench: LLM judges on agentic tool calls

Without ground truth, 6 judges plateau at 77-82% on hard tool-calling cases. Rubrics add at most 6.5 pp. CoT and temperature had negligible effect.
Keep the $500 rule in a code metric.
arXiv 2608.26623 AgentJudgeBench
AgentJudgeBench, from August 2026, tests LLM judges on agentic tool-calling cases at several difficulty levels. Without ground truth, all six judges converge to 77 to 82 percent alignment on the hard cases, a structural ceiling. Structured rubrics help by at most 6.5 points, and chain of thought or temperature had negligible effect. The dots are schematic: they show where the six judges land, all inside the reported band. For the Acme gate this is the reason the 500 dollar rule is a code metric: a rule that must hold every time cannot sit on an instrument that is wrong about one case in five. Analogy: a referee who is right four times out of five is fine for style points, not for the goal line. A likely question: "Will a bigger judge fix it?" The paper saw the plateau across judges, so the fix is a different kind of check, not a bigger judge.
arXiv Sep 2026

A pinned temperature-0 judge still flips 40% of close calls

arXiv 2609.33044 2026-09-27

Pinned and Still Unstable: within-judge verdict variance

The same judge, same input, temperature 0, flips ~5% of verdicts on reruns and ~40% on close calls.
num_samples 5 per case and num_runs ≥ 3 per change.
arXiv 2609.33044 Pinned and Still Unstable
Pinned and Still Unstable, from September 2026, reruns the same judge on the same inputs with temperature 0 and a pinned model version. About 5 percent of verdicts still flip between reruns, and on close calls, the cases near the decision line, about 40 percent flip. The tiles are schematic: four clear items with 2 flips in 40 verdicts, which is 5 percent, and one close call that flips 4 of 10 times. For the Acme gate this means two things: sample the judge 5 times per case with num_samples, and judge a change by at least three runs, with AgentEvaluator num_runs, because adk eval has no repeat flag in 2.13.0. Analogy: a bathroom scale that reads 70 or 71 kilos on the same morning; weigh three times before you celebrate. A likely question: "Is temperature 0 not deterministic?" Not in practice: the paper measured these flips with temperature 0 and a pinned model.
Build · Monday change from GAUGE

Add a judge-free completion bit next to every rubric

labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/completion_bit.py · excerpt
from google.adk.evaluation.eval_case import get_all_tool_calls
from google.adk.evaluation.evaluator import (
    EvalStatus, EvaluationResult)

DONE = {"escalate_to_human", "issue_refund"}   # terminal tools

def completion_bit(eval_metric, actual_invocations,
                   expected_invocations, conversation_scenario):
    done = any(call.name in DONE for inv in actual_invocations
               for call in get_all_tool_calls(inv.intermediate_data))
    status = EvalStatus.PASSED if done else EvalStatus.FAILED
    return EvaluationResult(overall_score=1.0 if done else 0.0,
                            overall_eval_status=status)
refund_agent/sim_config.json · merged in
"completion_bit": 1.0
},
"custom_metrics": {"completion_bit": {
  "code_config": {"name":
    "completion_bit.completion_bit"}}},

Done means a terminal tool was called.

Read the tool calls, not the words. No judge.

Set the status, as in refund_policy_score.

Completion is not correctness. Keep the rubric and the $500 metric.

The Monday change from GAUGE: a judge-free completion bit for the simulated set. The rule is simple: the chat is done only if the agent called a terminal tool, escalate_to_human or issue_refund; nothing a judge says can change that. The function reads the tool calls with get_all_tool_calls, sets the score and the status, and is registered like refund_policy_score, with the threshold under criteria and the import path under custom_metrics in sim_config.json. Completion is not correctness: a refund of 820 dollars is "complete", so keep refund_policy_score and the rubric next to it. Analogy: the parcel tracking says "delivered", whatever the customer email says. A likely question: "Why not check the final text for a ticket id?" You can, but tool calls are structured data, while text can mention a ticket that was never opened.
In production Shopify Sidekick

Shopify calibrated its judge from kappa 0.02 to 0.61

labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/judge_kappa.py · excerpt
import csv
import sys
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

path = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "labels.csv"
with open(path, newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))  # chat_id, human, judge
kappa = cohen_kappa_score([r["human"] for r in rows],
                          [r["judge"] for r in rows])
print(f"{len(rows)} chats, kappa = {kappa:.2f}")

Kappa is agreement beyond chance: 0 is chance, 1 is perfect.

Ground truth: sampled real chats, each labelled by 3 or more experts.

Acme: label about 100 refund chats before the judge gates anything.

Post Shopify Engineering, 2025-08-26
Cohen's kappa measures agreement beyond chance: 0 is chance and 1 is perfect. Shopify's first Sidekick judge agreed with expert labels at a kappa of 0.02, which is close to chance; after calibration it reached 0.61, against a human ceiling of 0.69, the agreement between the experts themselves. The labels came from sampled real conversations, each labelled by at least 3 experts, and their swap test is simple: put a human into the judge group, and if people cannot tell who the judge is, trust it. The script on the right is the check you can run yourself: label about 100 refund chats, run the judge on the same chats, and compute kappa with scikit-learn; the lab has a labels.csv with sample rows. Analogy: you calibrate a scale with known weights before you weigh parcels with it. A likely question: "When is the judge good enough?" When its kappa nears the human ceiling; stop tuning there, because the humans do not agree more than that.
In production Rippling

Rippling layers its evals from every commit to production

every commitrefund.evalset.json, 2 golden cases
post-mergerefund_sim, simulated customers
blocks deployrefund_policy_score 1.0, exit 1
productionfailing traces become new cases

Right: the same layers for the Acme refund gate. Vendor case study, 2026-06-01.

Case study Rippling on LangChain
Rippling, in a vendor case study from June 2026, layers its agent evals like a pyramid. The base is offline tests with mocks on every commit. Above it, 300 to 400 integration queries run after merge in a full sandbox. About ten scenarios block a deploy. At the top, evals run continuously in production, several times a day. Step two closes the loop: failing production traces go back to the base, an agent proposes a fix, the evals rerun, and a human merges. The table maps the same layers onto the Acme refund gate we built: the golden set on every commit, the simulated set after merge, the 500 dollar metric as the deploy blocker, and production failures as new golden cases. The numbers are Rippling's own and come from a vendor post, so read them as a shape, not a benchmark. Analogy: a test pyramid for code, with a feedback pipe from the top back to the base. A likely question: "Why only ten blocking scenarios?" A deploy gate must be fast and trusted; the broad suites inform, the few hard cases block.
Best practices · 1 of 2

Score hard rules in code, and only meaning with a judge

  • The $500 rule is a code metric.
  • Judges score meaning: pinned model, 5 samples.
  • A completion bit beside every rubric.
  • Rubrics state the procedure, not golden ids.
  • No reference metrics on simulated cases.
2608.26623Judges plateau at 77-82% on hard tool calls.
2609.33044A pinned judge flips ~40% of close calls.
2609.1219157.5% of "satisfied" chats failed the task.
2609.30471Golden-id judges failed 100% of correct off-reference answers.
ADK 2.13.0expected_invocations is needed by this metric.
The first half of the checklist for the Acme refund eval gate: what to score. Hard rules such as the 500 dollar ceiling go into a code metric, because judges plateau at 77 to 82 percent on hard tool-calling cases. Use the judge only for meaning, with a pinned model and five samples, because a pinned judge still flips about 40 percent of close calls. Put a judge-free completion bit beside every rubric, because 57.5 percent of "satisfied" simulated chats had failed. Write rubrics that describe the procedure, not the golden values: the CARGO paper, arXiv 2609.30471, found a reference-based judge failed every correct answer about an entity that differed from the golden one. And keep reference metrics off simulated cases, which have no golden turns; ADK fails with "expected_invocations is needed by this metric." Analogy: use a ruler for lengths and a person for taste, never the other way round. A likely question: "Does this mean one metric per rule?" Yes: small, named metrics make a red run easy to read.
Best practices · 2 of 2

Run each eval three times and test the gate itself

  • Run ≥ 3 times. Accept by paired bootstrap.
  • Trust one run.
  • Check the config path and the case count.
  • Keep a known-bad case per gate.
  • Pin agent, judge and harness. 43 → 72 solved by harness alone.
labs/adk/lab9-refund-eval/test_refund.py · pytest -q
import pytest
from google.adk.evaluation.agent_evaluator import AgentEvaluator

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_refund_golden():
    await AgentEvaluator.evaluate(
        agent_module="refund_agent",
        eval_dataset_file_path_or_dir=
            "refund_agent/refund.evalset.json",
        num_runs=3)   # default is 2
arXiv 2609.32092 paired bootstrap arXiv 2608.26218 harness
The second half of the checklist: how often to run, and how to trust the gate itself. adk eval has no repeat flag in 2.13.0, so run the golden set from pytest with AgentEvaluator and num_runs 3; the default is 2. Accept a change only by a paired bootstrap, as the production shopping-assistant paper arXiv 2609.32092 does: resample the same cases from the old and new runs many times and check that the confidence interval of the score change stays above zero. Never trust one run, because close calls flip about 40 percent of the time. Then test the gate: check the config path, count the cases, keep a known-bad case that must fail, and pin the agent model, the judge model and the harness version, because changing only the harness took the same model from 43 to 72 solved SWE-bench tasks in arXiv 2608.26218. Analogy: a smoke alarm is only useful if you test it with smoke. A likely question: "Is three runs enough?" For a gate, yes, as a floor; for a leaderboard-style comparison of close agents, you need far more.

Take the Acme HR assistant to production: guard it, trace it, ship it, canary it, roll it back.

This chapter takes the Acme People Team HR assistant from a laptop to production, and every station on the track is one lab or build-up. We guard it with our own plugin and Model Armor, trace it without putting employee data into spans, deploy it to Agent Runtime, Cloud Run or GKE, canary the new revision, publish it to Gemini Enterprise, and observe it. Watch the red arc in the animation: when tokens per invocation go above 1.5 times the baseline, which is the signature of a loop, we roll back in one command and the loop starts again. Think of it as a pit lane in a race: the car goes out, the team watches the telemetry, and a bad lap brings it straight back in. A likely question: "Why not just use the Model Armor settings in the Gemini Enterprise console?" Because those settings do not protect ADK agents, so the guards must live in the agent code. Lab 10 Acme HR assistant · step 1 of 3

HrGuardPlugin redacts SSNs and refuses other employees' bands

labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/hr_agent/agent.py · excerpt
SSN = re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b")

class HrGuardPlugin(BasePlugin):       # __init__: name="hr_guard"
    async def before_model_callback(self, *, callback_context,
                                    llm_request):
        for content in llm_request.contents or []:
            for part in content.parts or []:
                if part.text and SSN.search(part.text):
                    part.text = SSN.sub("[REDACTED-SSN]", part.text)
        return None                    # None = continue
    async def before_tool_callback(self, *, tool, tool_args,
                                   tool_context):
        caller = tool_context.state.get("employee_id")
        if (tool.name == "get_salary_band"
                and tool_args.get("employee_id") != caller):
            return {"status": "error", "error_message":
                    "You can only view your own salary band."}

Rewrite each SSN in place, then return None: the model call goes on.

A returned dict replaces the tool result. The tool never runs.

Plugin hooks are keyword-only, and the name is tool_args.

adk web · output · illustrative
user> What is the salary band of E-2002?
[execute_tool get_salary_band] ->
 {"status":"error","error_message":
  "You can only view your own salary band."}
agent> I'm sorry, I can only share your own band.
Our own HrGuardPlugin is the outer ring: plain, deterministic code that runs before the model and before every tool. Press once: before_model_callback walks every part of the request and rewrites any SSN to REDACTED-SSN in place; returning None means "continue", so the model still runs, only on clean text. Press again: before_tool_callback compares the employee id in the tool arguments with the caller's id in session state; a returned dict replaces the tool result, so get_salary_band never runs for E-2002. Press again: the illustrative output shows the error dict and the polite reply. Plugin hooks are keyword-only and the argument is tool_args; an agent-level before_tool_callback gets args instead, which is a common copy-paste bug. Analogy: the badge reader at the office door knows exactly which room you may enter. Likely question: "Why not let Model Armor do the salary check?" Authorization is a fixed rule that must hold every time, so it belongs in code; a classifier is the second layer. Full file: labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/hr_agent/agent.py.

    instruction=("Answer Acme HR policy questions. "

        prompt_template_name=template,

The managed ModelArmorPlugin is the inner ring, and App is where both rings meet. Press once: one template screens three paths, the prompt, the model reply and, new in this release, every tool output, which is the path indirect injection uses; watch the E-1001 call pass the own-id check, the L5 result pass the tool-output screen, and the reply pass the response screen. Press again: App takes the plugin list in order, so our deterministic guard runs before the classifier, and two plugins with the same name raise "already registered". The loader picks app before root_agent, so adk web finds the plugins without a code change. Press again: an injection prompt stops at the prompt screen and the user gets the default blocked message; block_on_screening_failure=True is the default, so an API error also blocks the turn. Analogy: the badge reader is our code, the security scanner inside is Model Armor; it looks for dangerous content but does not know the org chart. Likely question: "Why not set Model Armor in the Gemini Enterprise console?" Those settings do not protect ADK agents, so the plugin stays in code. Next: step 2 traces this guarded app.

Set up telemetry first, then import the app from step 1.

Step two of the Acme HR lab traces the guarded app from step one, and keeps employee data out of the spans. Press once: the three setdefault lines name the service and the environment, and turn content capture off; ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS defaults to on, so without this line every prompt and reply lands in every span, and the card on the right shows the question struck out. Press again: with no hooks, maybe_set_otel_providers still adds the generic OTLP exporter from OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT, for example Jaeger on port 4318; with TO_CLOUD=1 it sends OTLP over HTTP to telemetry.googleapis.com, which needs roles/telemetry.writer. Without the otel extra, export is disabled with only one warning, which is easy to miss. Press again: the app import comes after the setup lines. Analogy: a trace is a flight log many people can read; it records times and fuel, not the passengers' conversations. Likely question: "Where do I keep the full content for debugging?" In an access-controlled store, keyed by the trace id, not in the spans.
Lab 10 Acme HR assistant · step 2 of 3

Run one HR turn and read its trace: four spans, no call_llm

python hr_traced.pyTO_CLOUD=1 python hr_traced.py
labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/hr_traced.py · excerpt
async def main() -> None:
    runner = Runner(app=app, session_service=InMemorySessionService(),
                    auto_create_session=True)
    msg = types.Content(role="user",
        parts=[types.Part(text="What is my salary band?")])
    async for event in runner.run_async(
            user_id="E-1001", session_id="s1", new_message=msg,
            state_delta={"employee_id": "E-1001"}):  # guard input
        if event.is_final_response():
            print("agent>", event.content.parts[0].text)
    tp = trace.get_tracer_provider()  # BatchSpanProcessor queue
    if hasattr(tp, "force_flush"):    # ProxyTracerProvider has none
        tp.force_flush()

asyncio.run(main())

state_delta puts the caller's id in state. The guard checks it.

Flush before exit, or the last spans stay in the queue.

2.13 uses GenAI semconv 1.44: no call_llm span.

Only adk deploy agent_engine --otel_to_cloud turns content off for you.

Now we run one turn of the guarded app and read the trace it leaves. Press once: Runner takes the App from step one, so both guard plugins run; state_delta writes the caller's employee id into session state, which is what HrGuardPlugin compares with. Press again: spans leave through a BatchSpanProcessor, so a short script must flush before it exits; the hasattr check is there because with no exporter configured the global provider is a ProxyTracerProvider, which has no force_flush. Press again: the waterfall has four spans, invoke_agent, generate_content, execute_tool and a second generate_content; 2.13 defaults to the GenAI semantic conventions 1.44, which removed the call_llm span, so do not build a dashboard on it. Press again: with TO_CLOUD=1 the same waterfall shows in Cloud Trace. Only adk deploy agent_engine with --otel_to_cloud also turns content capture off; on Cloud Run and GKE you keep the env line from the last slide. Analogy: the waterfall is a stopwatch per lap, not a recording of the race. Likely question: "Why is call_llm missing from my old dashboard?" The schema changed in 2.13; the gotcha slides later show the fix. Durations on the slide are illustrative.

Lab 10 Acme HR assistant · step 3 of 3 · Cloud Run, GKE

The same folder ships to Cloud Run or GKE and stays private

labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/ship.sh · excerpt
# B) Cloud Run: private, one warm instance
adk deploy cloud_run --project=$PROJECT --region=$REGION \
  --service_name=acme-hr \
  --session_service_uri="agentengine://$AGENT_ENGINE_ID" \
  hr_agent -- --no-allow-unauthenticated --min-instances=1

# C) GKE: ClusterIP by default, no public IP

  --cluster_name=agents-prod --service_type=ClusterIP hr_agent

# also: --extra_packages (new in 2.13), --validate-agent-import
# --trace_to_cloud is deprecated

Flags after -- go to gcloud run deploy. Keep the service private.

Without --session_service_uri, sessions live in instance memory.

ClusterIP is the default. LoadBalancer gives a public IP.

Same package, three trade-offs. Pick by what you must run yourself.

The same folder goes to the two self-managed targets. Press once: adk deploy cloud_run passes everything after the double dash to gcloud run deploy, so we keep the service private with --no-allow-unauthenticated and keep one warm instance. Press again: --session_service_uri points sessions at the Agent Runtime instance from the last slide; without it they live in the container's memory and vanish when Cloud Run recycles the instance, which is the first gotcha later in this chapter. Press again: GKE gives a ClusterIP service by default, so nothing is public until you ask for a LoadBalancer. 2.13 also added --extra_packages for local packages, and --trace_to_cloud is deprecated in favour of --otel_to_cloud. Press again: the lists show the trade-off: Agent Runtime for managed sessions, Memory Bank and Gemini Enterprise; Cloud Run for the ADK FastAPI routes, revisions and your own session database; GKE for GPUs and self-hosted models. Analogy: one shipping container, three ports: a managed port, a self-service dock and your own warehouse. Likely question: "Can I mix them?" Yes, as here: Cloud Run serves, Agent Runtime stores the sessions.

Not by default: the ClusterIP service is reachable only inside the cluster, for example through kubectl port-forward.

Build · Acme HR assistant

Canary a new revision behind an eval run on its tagged URL

terminal · google-adk 2.13.0
$ adk deploy cloud_run --project=$PROJECT --region=$REGION \
    --service_name=acme-hr hr_agent
# the new revision takes 100% of the traffic at once
labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/canary.sh · excerpt
# 1. new revision at 0% traffic; the tag gets its own URL
$ gcloud run deploy acme-hr --image IMAGE_URL --no-traffic --tag cand
# 2. eval the live candidate before any user reaches it
$ agents-cli eval run --url https://cand---acme-hr-xyz.a.run.app
# 3. shift traffic; hold while the guard metrics stay steady
$ gcloud run services update-traffic acme-hr --to-revisions REV_NEW=5
$ gcloud run services update-traffic acme-hr --to-revisions REV_NEW=25
# 4. rollback: tokens per invocation > 1.5x baseline (a loop)
$ gcloud run services update-traffic acme-hr --to-revisions REV_PREV=100

--no-traffic --tag: the revision is live, but no user reaches it.

The evals hit the real deployed revision on its own URL.

5% of the traffic. All four gauges hold.

At 25%, tokens per invocation pass 1.5x. A loop burns tokens, not errors.

One command sends 100% back to the old revision.

The before line is the default: adk deploy cloud_run creates a new revision and it takes all the traffic at once, with no eval on the live URL. Press once: deploy with --no-traffic and a tag; the candidate is live and has its own URL, but no user reaches it. Press again: point agents-cli eval run --url at that URL, so the evals hit the real deployed revision. Press again: shift 5% and hold while error rate, p99 latency, tokens per invocation and the judge score stay steady; write these four guard metrics down before the launch. Press again: at 25% the tokens gauge passes 1.5 times the baseline; that is the agent-specific signal, because a loop does not raise errors, it burns tokens. Press again: the rollback is one update-traffic command back to the previous revision. Analogy: a new chef cooks for one table before the whole room. Likely question: "What if the evals pass but users still suffer?" That is why the gauges watch live traffic at each step; the eval run is the gate, the gauges are the guard. Gauge values are illustrative.
Gotcha Rollout on Agent Runtime

Agent Runtime has no traffic split: switch resources blue/green

SymptomYou look for a traffic split on Agent Runtime and find none. CauseNo traffic-split or revision-rollback feature was found for Agent Runtime. FixDeploy a second resource. Switch the client to its id. Switch back to roll back.
  • Soak and roll out every system-prompt change gradually.
  • Never shadow a candidate that has live write tools. Stub them.
Acme HR clientholds one id
resource 111old · live
resource 222new · evals pass
Postmortem Anthropic: an update on recent Claude Code quality reports Docs Cloud Run rollouts, rollbacks and traffic migration
The canary on the last slide uses Cloud Run revisions; Agent Runtime does not give you that. Press once: the research found no traffic-splitting or revision-rollback feature for Agent Runtime, so do not look for a percentage slider. Press again: deploy a second Agent Runtime resource for the new version and run the evals against it while the old one stays live. Press again: the client switches to the new resource id; to roll back, it switches back, so keep the old resource until the new one has soaked. Press again: two rules from production. Anthropic's 2026-04-23 postmortem added soak periods and gradual rollout for every system-prompt change. And never shadow-test a candidate that has live write tools: a shadow call to an HR or refund write tool is a real write, so stub those tools. Analogy: blue/green is two stages in one theatre; the audience walks to the second stage only when it is ready. Likely question: "How does the client switch?" Keep the resource id in config, not in code, so the switch is a config change.
Gotcha Deployment · 1 of 3

Cloud Run forgets the HR conversation without a session service

SymptomAn employee loses the conversation after a scale event. CauseNo --session_service_uri: the container "falls back to the in-memory session and artifact services". FixPoint sessions at Agent Runtime, or at a SQLAlchemy URL.
labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/ship.sh · excerpt
adk deploy cloud_run --project=$PROJECT --region=$REGION \
  --service_name=acme-hr \
  --session_service_uri="agentengine://$AGENT_ENGINE_ID" \
  hr_agent -- --no-allow-unauthenticated
E-1001same session
instance As1 in memory
instance Bempty memory
s1 lostA recycled
sessionsAgent Runtime
This is the first of three deploy defaults that bite the Acme HR assistant in its first production week. Press once: turn 1 of the conversation lands on instance A, and turn 2 lands on a new instance B after a scale event. Press again: Cloud Run recycled instance A, and without a session service URI the container keeps sessions in memory, so session s1 is gone; the ADK docs say the container "falls back to the in-memory session and artifact services" and loses them when an instance is recycled. Press again: the fix is one flag: --session_service_uri with agentengine:// and the Agent Runtime id, or a SQLAlchemy URL for your own database; now both instances read and write the same store. Analogy: a waiter who keeps the order in his head goes home at the end of the shift; write the order on the ticket. Likely question: "Does min-instances=1 fix it?" No: a warm instance still restarts and scales out, so keep the state outside the container. The same logic applies to --artifact_service_uri for files.
Gotcha Deployment · 2 of 3 · cli_deploy.py L1893-1898

Each agent_engine deploy without an id makes a new instance

SymptomTwo instances exist. The client still talks to the old one. CauseWithout --agent_engine_id, every deploy creates a new instance. A failed update deletes only a newly created one. FixPass --agent_engine_id on every update.
labs/adk/c10-acme-hr/ship.sh · excerpt
adk deploy agent_engine --project=$PROJECT --region=$REGION \
  --agent_engine_id=$AGENT_ENGINE_ID hr_agent
The second default is on Agent Runtime. Press once: CI runs adk deploy agent_engine three times without an instance id; each run creates a new instance, so we end with three instances while the HR web client still talks to instance 1 on revision 1. Press again: the cause is in cli_deploy.py: without --agent_engine_id, every deploy creates a new instance, and if an update fails, only a newly created instance is deleted, so the old ones stay and keep billing. Press again: pass --agent_engine_id on every update and the deploy updates instance 1 in place; the client gets revision 3 at the same address. Analogy: the instance id is a house number; without it the mover builds a new house each time instead of furnishing the one you live in. Likely question: "How do I clean up the extra instances?" Delete them in the console or with the Agent Platform SDK, and put the id in your CI variables so it cannot be forgotten.

Tracing is on in the Acme HR assistant, and three telemetry defaults now work against us; this is the first. ADK copies the message content into spans unless ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS is false; the default lives in telemetry/context.py. Press once: only adk deploy agent_engine with --otel_to_cloud sets it to false for you; on Cloud Run and on GKE it stays on. Press again: on Cloud Run, pass the env var to gcloud after the double dash with --set-env-vars. Press again: on Agent Runtime, --otel_to_cloud already does it. Keep it in an access-controlled store keyed by the trace id, not in spans that the whole ops team can read.

SymptomPanels keyed on call_llm read 0 after the upgrade. No error. Cause2.13.0 defaults to GenAI semconv 1.44. The Cloud Trace docs still list call_llm. FixRebuild panels on generate_content, or opt out for now.
opt out · only while old panels need the v1 names
export ADK_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA_VERSION_OPT_IN=\
otel_semconv_1_36
The second telemetry default is a silent schema change. Press once: watch the two panels across the upgrade; the call_llm panel drains to zero and nothing raises an error, while a panel rebuilt on generate_content fills from the same traffic. Press again: the CHANGELOG for 2.13.0 says the default schema is now the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions 1.44, and that schema has no call_llm span; the Cloud Trace integration docs still list call_llm, so the docs mislead you here. Press again: the right fix is to rebuild the panels on generate_content; the temporary fix is ADK_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA_VERSION_OPT_IN=otel_semconv_1_36, which restores the v1 names. Analogy: the city renamed the street; the traffic is still there, but your map no longer finds it. Likely question: "How do I notice a silent zero next time?" Alert when spans are ingested but the panel metric is zero, and run one synthetic query per deploy. Bar heights are illustrative.
Gotcha Telemetry · 3 of 3

Tracing fails quietly: alert when spans arrive but metrics stay zero

SymptomCauseFix
No ADK spansPhoenix or Langfuse set a global TracerProvider first. ADK's set is "a no-op and results in a warning".Register one provider. Add the extra processors to it.
MCP calls untracedMCP SDK 2.x. The instrumentor is built for httpx 1.x.Expect no MCP spans on SDK 2.x.
Panels read 02.2.0 sent cloud.resource.id, not cloud.resource_id. Fixed in 2.4.0.Alert on spans > 0 with metric = 0.
Docs ADK Cloud Trace Repo adk-python #6247
The last telemetry gotchas share one pattern: nothing errors, the numbers just stop. Press once: if Phoenix or Langfuse installs a global TracerProvider before ADK, ADK's own set call is "a no-op and results in a warning", so ADK spans never appear; register one provider and add the extra span processors to it. Press again: with MCP SDK 2.x, MCP calls go untraced, because the instrumentor is built for httpx 1.x; know this gap before you debug an MCP tool from traces. Press again: 2.2.0 sent cloud.resource.id instead of cloud.resource_id, so dashboards keyed on the right name read zero until 2.4.0 fixed it. The defence for all three is the alert at the bottom: spans are ingested, but the metric is zero. Analogy: a smoke detector with a dead battery is silent too; test it on purpose. Likely question: "How do I test the alert?" Send one synthetic query per deploy and check that both counters move. The counter values are illustrative.

Origin checks in code beat injection detectors that do not transfer

origin_guard.py · simplified sketch of ROPE
SENSITIVE = {"send_email": ["to"], "transfer_funds": ["iban", "amount"]}

async def origin_guard(tool, args, tool_context):
    fields = SENSITIVE.get(tool.name, [])
    # filled by YOUR code from the user turn / CRM
    trusted = set(tool_context.state.get("user:trusted_values", []))
    for f in fields:
        if str(args.get(f)) not in trusted:
            return {"status": "blocked",  # returned dict skips the tool
                    "error": f"'{f}' did not originate from the user or a trusted record; "
                             "ask the user to confirm"}
    return None

Three papers from August to October point the same way: put the security decision in code, and treat classifiers as an extra filter. Step 1: a 14-vector test of multi-agent systems found that injection through tool output succeeded 43% of the time even with system-prompt guardrails, and that role-scoped tools plus boundary screening cut overall success from 31.2% to 4.2%. Steps 2 and 3: ROPE guards only the few parameters that move money or data, and admits a value only if it came from the user or a trusted record, so the attacker can reword the injection five times and the gate gives the same answer; that is where the 1.6 to 2.6% attack success comes from. Step 4: detectors picked by public benchmark scores do not transfer, and the BIPIA leader catches 2% of AgentDojo injections at 1% false positives. Analogy: a bank checks that the payee is on your saved list; it does not try to guess if the phone call sounds suspicious. A likely question is "So is Model Armor useless?": no, it is a second layer on prompts, replies and tool outputs, but measure its false-positive rate on your own Contoso tool outputs before you turn on blocking. Next: two production teams that treat agent and prompt changes as reviewed, gated deploys.

ROPE, from August, makes the security decision in code instead of asking a model to spot the attack. Press once: without a gate, a web page returned by a tool carries an injected IBAN ending 6666, the agent copies it into transfer_funds, and the money goes to the attacker. Press again: the origin gate checks only the sensitive parameter: a value passes only if your code saw it in the user turn or in a trusted record, so the user's IBAN ending 1001 passes and the injected one stops; the paper reports attack success of 1.6 to 2.6% while keeping 82 to 100% of the clean utility. Press again: the attacker rewords the injection five times and the gate gives the same answer every time, because it never reads the wording, only where the value came from. The action for Monday: list the five to ten parameters that move money or data out of Acme and guard only those. Analogy: a bank checks that the payee is on your saved list; it does not judge whether the phone call sounds suspicious. Likely question: "Where does the trusted list come from?" From your own code: the parsed user turn and your CRM, never from model output. The next slide shows the hook.

Contoso: the agent explores, the maintainer subtracts. Ship prompt and harness changes through the eval-gated canary, like code.
The best engineering case for ADK comes from the ADK team itself: they let Gemini 4 Argon work on the ADK Python codebase for 11 hours with a goal prompt that asked for an unmerged PR with before and after numbers. Step 1: it built a baseline of 4 workloads with 30 runs each and proposed 6 changes across 32 files. Step 2: maintainers shipped 2 and rejected 4; one rejected change passed all 16,892 open-source tests but broke 25 internal Google test targets, and a 17% cache gain held only on a synthetic benchmark. Step 3: the shipped work made a 158-turn run drop from 65.6 to 56.1 seconds, and the post adds an ops tip: warm up each new instance before it takes live traffic. Step 4: Anthropic's April postmortem shows the other side; three small harness and prompt changes passed review, tests and dogfooding and still lowered quality, so they now run per-model evals on every prompt change, soak and roll out gradually. Analogy: a junior engineer who works all night is useful, but a senior still reviews the pull request. A likely question is "Which Contoso changes count as deploys?": the instruction, the model id, plugin config and tool descriptions all go through the same eval and canary as code. Post Optimizing a 200,000-line Python codebase overnight
The best engineering case for ADK comes from the ADK team itself: they let Gemini 4 Argon work on the ADK Python codebase for 11 hours, with a goal prompt that asked for an unmerged pull request with before and after numbers, guided by a SKILL.md index in .agents/skills. Press once: it built a baseline of 4 workloads with 30 runs each and proposed 6 changes across 32 files. Press again: the maintainers shipped 2 and rejected 4; one rejected change passed all 16,892 open-source tests but broke 25 internal Google test targets, and a 17% cache gain held only on a synthetic benchmark. Press again: the two shipped changes, a 21% faster cold import and about 40% less session preparation, made a 158-turn run drop from 65.6 to 56.1 seconds; the post adds an ops tip that fits our canary: warm up each new instance before it takes live traffic. Analogy: a junior engineer who works all night is useful, but a senior still reviews the pull request. Likely question: "Would our tests have caught the rejected change?" Only if they cover what the internal targets covered; that is why a human review and a canary stay in the loop.
Best practices

Production checklist for the Contoso HR assistant, item by item

1 · Versions and release

  • Pin google-adk==2.13.0, mcp, a2a-sdk, litellm. Canary each minor. 13 minors in 5 months; 2.2.0, 2.7.0, 2.11.0 regressed.
  • Gate deploys on adk eval and a canary. Exits 1 on failure.
  • --agent_engine_id on every update. Else a new instance.

2 · Security and privacy

  • Auth in front of adk api_server. None by default.
  • Cloud Run: --no-allow-unauthenticated. Identity tokens.
  • ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS=false off Agent Runtime. Default: on.
  • --with_ui in production. "ADK Web is for development purposes."
  • Gemini Enterprise console Model Armor. Not for ADK agents.

3 · Operations

  • Deploy with --session_service_uri, --artifact_service_uri. Else: lost sessions.
  • Warm-up request before live traffic. Pays the import cost.
  • Cost per successful outcome; tokens per invocation. Loops show as tokens.
  • Idempotency keys on side effects. Resume is at-least-once.

This slide is the release checklist for the Contoso HR assistant, in three groups: versions and release, security and privacy, and operations. ADK shipped 13 minor releases in 5 months, and 2.2.0, 2.7.0 and 2.11.0 each brought a regression, so pin the same versions in local and deployed requirements and canary every upgrade. The two red items are traps: --with_ui puts the dev UI with access to all data in production, and the Gemini Enterprise console Model Armor settings do not protect ADK agents, so the guard must live in the agent code. Think of it like a pre-flight checklist: the pilot knows how to fly, but the list catches the step a tired person skips. A likely question is "Why track cost per successful outcome and not cost per call?" Because arXiv 2610.13092 found a cheaper, faster decision model that raised the mean cost per successful outcome in one agent.
